#5574. Google is unveiling two new specialized AI chips to widen its challenge to Nvidia

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The TPU 8tx and 8i Max, due to be available next year, target confidential computing and long-context AI workloads

Google $GOOGL is launching a pair of tailored tensor processing units, or TPUs, to expand its AI chip lineup against Nvidia $NVDA, according to Bloomberg. The TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max will be unveiled Monday, with availability set for next year, Google chip chief Amin Vahdat told Bloomberg.

The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. Vahdat said that matters for drug discovery, math and coding. The chip packs two TPU chips together, giving it extra processing muscle and memory.

Both variations are reconfigured versions of existing silicon rather than new designs, Vahdat said. Google changed them to handle tasks customers have requested. They follow two TPU models Google released this year, according to Bloomberg, which said the chip unit used to release one new processor every two years.

"We could build a single chip that tries to address the whole market, or by building specialized versions of the chips, we actually can deliver much more value," Vahdat said, according to Bloomberg.

Google's TPUs compete with Nvidia's graphics processing units. Customers include Apple $AAPL, Meta $META Platforms and Oracle $ORCL, according to Bloomberg. Anthropic holds the right to acquire up to $150 billion of TPUs from 2028 through 2031, according to Bloomberg, which cited a regulatory filing.

Nvidia is also moving toward specialization, according to Bloomberg. It offers its own central processing units and inference-focused chips that use technology from startup Groq.

Oracle and Google said in October that TPUs will be available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in calendar year 2027. That marks the first time the chips will be offered on a hyperscale cloud platform other than Google's own. Google designs its chips with Broadcom $AVGO and manufactures them at TSMC $TSM.

Supply is tight. Every TPU unit Google has is already committed to a customer, the company said in its earnings report, according to Bloomberg. Google faces shortages of memory and manufacturing capacity and is seeking to diversify its suppliers, Bloomberg said. Vahdat declined to comment on the role of Marvell Technology or MediaTek in the TPU business.

#5573. What NAR’s new MLS policy options mean for data feeds and licensing

NAR adopted 4 MLS policy recommendations at NAR NXT 2026, including an optional policy that lets MLSs seek up to 50% copyright interest in certain listing content with opt outs. Additional updates address local rules for data feeds, permitted uses tied to brokerage or valuation services, and MLS Committee qualifications.  AI Summary

The National Association of Realtors (NAR) has approved four multiple listing service (MLS) policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee.

The recommendations from NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee were considered and adopted at NAR NXT 2026 conference on Sunday and are tied to the trade group’s 2026-2028 strategic plan to modernize MLS policies, the association said in an announcement Sunday.

The most consequential change for brokers and MLS operators is a revision to MLS Policy Statement 7.85 and the creation of a new optional policy on copyright protection of MLS data.

Under the revised policy, MLSs may, at their discretion, require up to a 50% copyright interest in certain listing content to strengthen copyright enforcement, subject to quarterly copyright registration requirements. MLSs must give participants the right to opt out of assigning a copyright interest to the MLS, and brokers retain the right to independently use and license their own listing content.

Copyright ownership and enforcement have become more important as listing photos and data are syndicated across portals, IDX sites and marketing platforms, and as MLSs face more frequent questions and disputes about unauthorized scraping and reuse of listing content.

NAR also adopted an optional MLS policy on MLS data feed services. The policy allows MLSs to establish local eligibility and licensing requirements for data feeds, as long as those rules are reasonable, objective and applied equally to all participants.

Even with new local rules, participants must retain access to MLS listing information and data feeds for their own listings.

For brokers and vendors, this could affect how quickly and under what conditions they can obtain broader data feeds for tools such as brokerage websites, back-office systems and analytics products, depending on how individual MLSs choose to implement the optional policy.

A new MLS policy statement reinforces that the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and must be connected to real estate brokerage services, the preparation of appraisals or other valuations of real property.

NAR said this is intended to address concerns around unauthorized use of MLS content, including use cases that are not connected to providing brokerage or valuation services.

For MLSs, this language provides additional backing for enforcement actions against parties that use listing data for unrelated commercial purposes. For brokers and appraisers, it underscores the need to align technology partnerships and data workflows with the scope of their MLS agreements.

NAR also updated the qualification criteria for service on its MLS Committee. The changes are meant to better reflect today’s MLS environment and ensure the committee includes members with relevant industry expertise and perspectives.

While specific qualification details were not outlined in the announcement, changes to committee composition can influence how future policy recommendations are shaped and how regional and business-model interests are represented at the national level.

“These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective, and responsive to the needs of today’s real estate industry,” Nykia Wright, the CEO of NAR and a 2026 HousingWire Woman of Influence and Vanguard award winner, said in the announcement. “In line with our 2026–2028 Strategic Plan and significant member feedback, we will continue working collaboratively with MLSs, brokers, members, and other industry partners to support a clear understanding and implementation of these changes.”

Because several of the policies are optional, local MLSs will have to decide whether and how to adopt them. MLS executives and boards will likely review their copyright strategies, data feed agreements and committee engagement structures in light of the new framework.

Brokers, teams and technology vendors should review their MLS participation and data licensing agreements to understand how any local policy changes could affect website data feeds, marketing uses of listing content and third-party integrations.

#5572. Google advances agentic AI custom silicon expanding TPU family with 8tx and 8i Max

Google LLC today introduced two new specialized silicon chips for artificial intelligence to its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit architecture family, aimed at higher compute density and secure inference.

At Google Cloud Next 2026 in April, Google introduced two specialized TPUs in the same generation, 8t for large-scale training and 8i designed for real-time reasoning. At the time, the company said it released the chips to handle demanding AI workloads across two primary tasks: building the models and running them.

Today’s expansion includes two new specialized chips across additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest possible compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx designed for secure and confidential inference.

Google said TPU 8i Max aims to scale compute and memory, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the high-bandwidth memory of TPU 8i. This gives processors as much memory as possible to handle data without swapping it out.

Additionally, the company added that 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the same rack footprint, lowering the floor space it takes per square foot and per watt in data centers.

This allows the new eighth-generation TPUs to provide customers with a purpose-built accelerator for larger models and the industry’s current push toward ultra-large context windows.

A context window acts as an AI model’s working space: how much data it can consider while answering a question. A larger window lets it work across a longer document, conversation history, audio file, video or collection of code. But expanding it comes at a cost. Processing and repeatedly consulting more information puts greater demands on chips to swap data in and out, requiring more on-chip memory and stronger connections that move data between processors.

Adding more on-chip memory reduces the need to move data between processors, lowering latency and reducing the power an AI model needs to “think” about information.

Google said it developed 8i Max alongside pushing massive context windows for its Gemini frontier model, which supports the 1 million-token industry standard. That represents roughly 750,000 words or 1,500 pages of text. Although flagship models tackle 1 million tokens, smaller models often support narrower window sizes between 128,000 and 256,000 tokens.

Google said it optimized TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference, designing the chip for regulated enterprises and governments that want to run frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside the most sensitive data.

Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but when an AI model processes that same information, it must be decoded. Built on the same architecture as the TPU 8t, with custom AMD central processing unit hosts, the 8tx builds in a secure enclave directly into the hardware layer that keeps sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated.

The company said the architecture pairs training-grade compute with fast inference, meaning organizations can run and customize models on a single confidential system. The combination allows regulated services and industries to fine-tune models using private data, distill large models into smaller ones and train agents through reinforcement learning.

All of this can be done without migrating data between separate clusters, which could expose sensitive information to leaks.

#5570. FAA brought first digital air traffic control towers online in the U.S.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Digital towers are operating at Bartow Executive Airport in Florida and Kenai Municipal Airport in Alaska, with five more planned

The Federal Aviation Administration announced that its first digital air traffic control towers are operational at airports in Florida and Alaska.

The systems are running at Bartow Executive Airport in Florida and Kenai Municipal Airport in Alaska, the agency said. Cameras and digital displays let controllers keep the whole airfield in sight without interruption, covering the full 360 degrees around it, from the runways and taxiways to the nearby skies. Controllers continue to manage the airspace, and the technology adds information to support their existing work, the FAA said.

"Our air traffic controllers continue to do the critical job of keeping aircraft safely separated, and we're giving them better technology to do that," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement.

Five non-towered airports will get digital towers with funding from President Donald Trump's Working Families Tax Cut Act, the FAA said. They are Winter Haven Regional Airport and Venice Municipal Airport in Florida, Montgomery County Airpark in Maryland, Johnston Regional Airport in North Carolina, and Durango-La Plata County Airport in Colorado.

The FAA said it conducted years of testing at the William J. Hughes Technical Center in Atlantic City, New Jersey, and other locations. The tests were meant to develop standards and confirm that digital tower systems meet the agency's safety, accuracy and reliability requirements. The agency selected the Frequentis system for deployment.

Bedford is scheduled to testify on Tuesday before the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee about the $12.5 billion push to overhaul how the nation controls air traffic, according to Reuters. He is expected to address how far the work has come and what obstacles remain in retiring outdated equipment, including paper flight strips, floppy disks and copper telecom lines.

In July 2025, lawmakers authorized $12.5 billion spread across five years to overhaul air traffic control, and the Trump administration is seeking an additional $30 billion, according to Reuters.

In September, the FAA began using an AI-powered air traffic management tool called SMART at Ronald Reagan Washington National, Dulles International and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall airports. The Transportation Department said at the time that the $12.5 billion in infrastructure upgrades is on track for completion by the end of 2028.

#5569. NAR sees pent-up demand waiting on lower mortgage rates, better sentiment

NAR economist Lawrence Yun said pent-up housing demand could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves, and confidence rebounds. NAR data show existing-home sales near 4M, first-time buyers at 22%, and months’ supply at its highest since 2015.  AI Summary

The U.S. housing market is building “significant” pent-up demand that could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves and consumer confidence rebounds, National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) chief economist Lawrence Yun told attendees Friday at NAR’s NXT in New Orleans.

Yun contrasted today’s sales environment with the year 2000, noting that the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million and payroll jobs from 132 million to 159 million over that period. Housing wealth has ballooned from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are tracking near 4 million this year, well below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000, he said, citing NAR data.

“Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said.

On the supply side, Yun said inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is now at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September, according to NAR.

“Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.”

Yun pointed to consumer psychology as a key missing ingredient. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the labor market has added jobs.

“If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said.

Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented findings from the trade group’s newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the series low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40.

Those numbers underscore how younger households are delaying homeownership, even as they form households and enter peak earning years. For lenders and real estate brokerages, that means fewer entry-level transactions and more emphasis on move-up or equity-rich buyers.

“First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They’re also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.”

Lautz noted that sellers reported staying in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest tenure on record for the survey.

“The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” she said. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.”

Despite technology and direct-to-consumer platforms, use of licensed professionals in transactions remained strong, according to NAR’s survey. A reported 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent.

“Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said.

For real estate agents and brokers, NAR’s data point to a market where transaction volume is constrained more by affordability, rates and sentiment than by underlying demand. A larger population, more jobs and higher housing wealth suggest that activity could accelerate quickly if mortgage rates retreat and confidence improves.

For lenders, a 22% first-time buyer share and a median first-time buyer age of 40 highlight both near-term headwinds and an eventual backlog of delayed demand. Households that are renting longer and juggling student debt and childcare may respond strongly to any easing in rates, pricing or down payment constraints.

For builders and developers, Lautz’s comments reinforce the policy and business case for adding affordable inventory. With existing owners locked in by sub-4% mortgages and staying put for a median 12 years, new construction remains one of the few levers to ease the entry-level shortage.

Yun’s and Lautz’s remarks come as the industry also adjusts to post-settlement commission rule changes and elevated borrowing costs, making accurate pricing, counseling on affordability and clear communication with consumers more central to winning business in 2027 and beyond.

#5567. Thieves stole $11.4 million in Nvidia hardware from Oakland shipment

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Six pallets bound for Fort Worth, Texas, disappeared after leaving Oakland on Aug. 29, and police have announced no arrests

Oakland police are investigating the theft of $11.4 million in Nvidia $NVDA hardware that disappeared after leaving Oakland for Fort Worth, Texas, on Aug. 29, according to ABC News.

The shipment consisted of six pallets. A truck linked to a food-hauling company collected the cargo on schedule, and investigators later lost its trail in San Bernardino County, California, according to ABC News.

The truck stopped repeatedly for hours at a stretch once the hardware was aboard, according to Ars Technica. The buyers realized in early September that the shipment had failed to arrive.

Oakland police said in a statement, according to ABC News: "The Oakland Police Department is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on Sept. 13, 2026." Authorities have announced no arrests, and the investigation is continuing.

Authorities have not disclosed the type of Nvidia hardware that was taken or the method the thieves used, according to Ars Technica.

Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business who studies artificial intelligence and emerging technology, told ABC News that Nvidia chips draw strong demand. "There's lots and lots of incentives to hijack those chips anywhere where security is weak," Groth said.

Groth said the chips sell for about double their U.S. price outside the country. "So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about $1 million or more abroad," he said, according to ABC News.

The Oakland case follows other attempts to steal Nvidia cargo in the Bay Area, according to ABC News. Police in Fremont and Union City looked into break-ins last year that targeted Nvidia cargo worth over $7.5 million. In a separate attempted theft in September, suspects who thought the trucks they were after held Nvidia technology instead found 40,000 pounds of sand, according to police cited by ABC News.

Thieves have taken upward of $100 million worth of cargo bound for data centers off the highways since June. Targeted goods include bitcoin mining rigs, servers, memory chips and fiber-optic cabling. In one of the largest heists, the thieves falsified tracking coordinates so electronic surveillance would not catch them.

The Oakland theft adds to a surge of hardware heists, according to Ars Technica. Ars Technica said thieves can dismantle the stolen components for resale on gray markets, or send them to countries where U.S. technology hardware may be off-limits.

#5566. Exclusive: FormAssembly overhauls its platform to expand into AI-powered process automation

FormAssembly Inc., a provider of online data collection and workflow automation software, today announced a complete platform overhaul that expands its capabilities beyond building forms to automating complex business processes using artificial intelligence.

The new platform, which the company said took seven months to develop, combines form creation, workflow automation, integrations and compliance management in a single no-code environment.

It also introduces conversational AI agents that can collect information through natural language interactions and support for the Model Context Protocol, enabling external AI agents to interact with FormAssembly’s software.

The launch marks a significant expansion for the 20-year-old company, which has traditionally focused on helping organizations collect structured information securely and integrate it into business applications. “We’re about how people share information with organizations and what happens after that,” said founder and Chief Executive Cedric Savarese.

The new platform builds on the AI assistant FormAssembly introduced last October, which enabled users to generate forms and configure workflows using natural language instructions. The latest release extends those capabilities to entire business processes, including approvals, document generation, electronic signatures and payments.

For example, a municipal government could describe an application process for obtaining a permit to hold an event in a public park. The platform’s assistant, called Fai, could then generate the necessary forms, approval workflows and documentation requirements.

“You can explain what you need in plain English to your agent, and the agent will build the entire process in a couple of minutes,” Savarese said.

FormAssembly claims the AI-assisted builder can reduce development time from days or weeks to minutes. Savarese said the company based those estimates on recreating existing customer workflows using the new platform.

A second major addition is conversational intake agents that replace traditional forms with interactive voice or text conversations. The agents use predefined data structures to guide conversations, answer questions and convert unstructured responses into information suitable for downstream systems.

The agents can also personalize interactions using previously collected information, although Savarese emphasized that access to that information is restricted by default.

FormAssembly uses frontier AI models, primarily from Anthropic PBC, rather than developing its own. Savarese said the company has zero-retention agreements with Anthropic and OpenAI Group PBC to protect customer information.

The revamped platform also adds governance capabilities that evaluate workflows against predefined compliance policies before publication. Organizations can use built-in rules or define their own requirements based on internal policies and applicable regulations. Potential violations are flagged for human review rather than automatically blocked.

MCP support and application programming interfaces enable customers to create and manage FormAssembly workflows through external systems without accessing the software’s traditional interface.

Savarese said this approach could protect established software companies from the risk that AI agents will make conventional software-as-a-service applications obsolete.

“People will use AI agents, but they use AI agents to drive software, not to replace it,” he said.

The company isn’t positioning itself as a comprehensive competitor to business process management vendors such as ServiceNow Inc. Instead, it intends to concentrate on processes that begin with collecting information from people.

Existing customers won’t be forced to migrate immediately. Savarese said migrations aren’t planned until January, and pricing for existing customers remains uncertain. More sophisticated automation capabilities could carry additional charges depending on customers’ current subscriptions.

FormAssembly, founded in 2006, raised its first outside funding of $10 million in 2019 after 13 years of bootstrapping. The company says it has thousands of customers, particularly in regulated industries such as healthcare, financial services, education and government.

#5565. The affordable housing we save is as important as the affordable housing we build

New York City’s housing plan targets 350,000 new homes and 100,000 preserved units in 5 years. A 2026 ANHD report finds 63,700 subsidized units in distress, and estimates replacement could require $10.2 billion to $26.8 billion in subsidies.   AI Summary

New York City needs approximately 700,000 new homes over the next decade. That’s the conclusion of the city’s recently released Fair Housing Growth Strategy, which establishes an ambitious framework for easing the affordability crisis in the City of New York.

The strategy sets five-year targets of 350,000 new homes and 100,000 preserved units. But we have to ask: Are we placing enough value on the housing we already have? Because, from an investment perspective, preservation may offer advantages that deserve considerably more attention.

The financial case is simple: Protecting an existing asset can require less capital than replacing it. New York City’s affordable housing inventory challenges provide an interesting case.

According to a 2026 report from the Association for Neighborhood & Housing Development, more than 63,700 subsidized affordable apartments are experiencing financial distress. The report estimates that replacing those units through new construction could require between $10.2 billion and $26.8 billion in public subsidies.

Those figures illustrate the potential financial consequences of allowing existing affordable housing to become unsustainable. Of course, not every distressed property will be lost, and not every building can be preserved economically. But the broader implication is clear. Every viable affordable property that can be preserved represents an important opportunity to protect existing housing capacity without incurring the full cost of replacement.

As we know, conventional real estate financing frequently relies on expectations of rental growth and asset appreciation. Affordable housing operates under a more stressed dynamic. On one hand, income restrictions limit revenue. On the other, maintenance, insurance, utilities and capital improvements continue to drive expenses.

These disparate realities can create financing gaps that conventional lenders and investors are unwilling or unable to absorb independently. And this is where public-private capital structures can make a substantial difference. By combining public subsidies, subordinate financing, private investment, tax incentives and long-term debt, preservation transactions can accommodate different financial objectives within a single investment.

Public capital can help reduce financing costs or absorb risks that would otherwise prevent a transaction from proceeding. Private capital can contribute investment capacity, underwriting discipline and long-term financing. Together, these sources can make preservation feasible while maintaining affordability commitments.

New York already employs variations of this approach to preserve its own large portfolio of aging housing. Facing aging buildings, constrained revenues and rising operating costs across its public housing portfolio, New York City has increasingly turned to public-private capital structures to support preservation and long-term affordability.

For example, the recently completed Reid Park Rock, a 1,696-unit, 87-building affordable housing development in East New York, redeveloped by Fairstead, BRB, LDCENY and NYHCA, cost approximately $375,000 per unit to acquire, restructure and completely modernize for the next generation. Financing partners included Vistria’s impact capital, Merchants Bank and a subordinate subsidy financing from the City of New York. The combination of public financing, expanded HUD rental subsidies and low-cost private capital made this possible.

By comparison, the cost of acquiring and developing this housing at scale today would far exceed these costs. Recently completed Innovative Urban Village, also in East New York, Brooklyn, reported a total of $270 million for 385 units, for an average of $700,000 per unit.

Similarly, Alafia Phase I, a 576-unit affordable property in East New York, recently delivered at $387 million or $672,000 per unit. Both projects required significant public subsidy, including low-income housing tax credits and subordinate low-cost subsidy loans from the state, but both came in at a staggering 80% higher per-unit development cost compared to the recently completed preservation of the Reid Park Rock partnership.

A successful preservation investment must provide sufficient resources for rehabilitation, support sustainable operations, establish appropriate reserves and maintain affordability over the intended investment horizon. That requires sophisticated capital structuring, but it also requires recognizing that an affordable housing asset’s value extends beyond immediate financial returns and ultimately serves as community infrastructure.

Preservation offers another important financial advantage: it can safeguard public and private capital that has already been deployed. Affordable housing developments frequently benefit from substantial public investment during their initial construction or rehabilitation. Those investments are intended to produce housing benefits over decades.

However, when a property becomes financially distressed or approaches the expiration of its affordability commitments, that original investment may no longer deliver its intended long-term value. Strategic reinvestment can facilitate the asset’s adjustment to the current regulatory and operational landscape, but also extend the property’s useful life, improve its financial performance and protect the affordability that the original capital helped create.

While some may view this as spending additional money on aging buildings, I see it much more as an exercise in investment stewardship. Especially because the alternative can be considerably more expensive.

New York unquestionably needs more housing construction. Preservation alone cannot create the additional inventory required to close the city’s overall supply gap. But new construction alone cannot guarantee that the city’s existing affordable housing opportunities will remain available. The two strategies must advance together.

The city’s 350,000-unit production target and 100,000-unit preservation target recognize that relationship. The challenge now is to ensure that preservation receives the same financial attention, investment expertise and execution capacity necessary to fulfill its role in this endeavor. Especially as the ANHD describes preserving existing subsidized housing as “the most practical and cost-effective strategy to maintain affordability in New York City.”

Ultimately, the success of New York’s affordable housing ambitions should be judged not only by the number of affordable homes created, but also by the number sustained.

Victoria Gousse is Principal and Chief Investment Officer at A. Walker & Co. This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5564. Roofing Expert Michael Majeski Identifies Snow and Ice Load Risks That Can Damage Winter Roofs

Michael Majeski, owner of Over The Top Roofing, explains how snow accumulation, ice dams, and preventive maintenance affect winter roof safety.

FULTON, N.Y., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How can homeowners protect their roofs from heavy snow and ice during Central New York winters? Michael Majeski, a roofing expert in Fulton, New York, explains how snow and ice loads affect roof safety in a HelloNation article. Michael Majeski owns Over The Top Roofing.

How Do Heavy Snow and Ice Loads Affect Roof Safety?

The HelloNation article explains that roofs are designed to support specific weight limits. When accumulated snow and ice exceed those limits, structural damage becomes a concern.

Wet, compacted snow weighs considerably more than light, powdery snow. The article emphasizes that homeowners should monitor accumulation rather than judge roof safety by snow depth alone.

Warning signs include sagging roof sections, cracked ceilings, and new leaks following winter storms. These conditions may indicate excessive structural stress requiring professional evaluation.

Why Do Ice Dams Cause Winter Roof Damage?

Ice dams develop when melted snow refreezes near roof edges. This frozen barrier can prevent additional melting snow from draining properly.

The HelloNation article explains that trapped water may move beneath shingles and enter attics or walls. Repeated moisture exposure can damage insulation, wood framing, and interior surfaces.

Michael Majeski, a roofing expert in Fulton, New York, highlights the importance of proper attic insulation and ventilation. Maintaining more consistent roof temperatures helps reduce the melting and refreezing that contributes to ice dam formation.

What Maintenance Helps Prevent Winter Roof Problems?

The article recommends inspecting roofs before winter to identify vulnerable areas around flashing, vents, and valleys. Addressing damaged shingles, deteriorating sealants, and existing leaks can reduce potential problems during storms.

Clean gutters also support drainage as snow melts. However, gutter cleaning alone cannot prevent ice dams caused by temperature differences between the roof and the air.

Homeowners may use roof rakes from the ground when conditions allow. The article cautions against climbing onto icy roofs because slippery surfaces create serious fall hazards.

When Should Homeowners Consider Professional Roof Evaluation?

Older roofs and structures exposed to repeated heavy snowfall may benefit from professional assessment.

The HelloNation article notes that some roofs may require structural reinforcement. Appropriate improvements depend on the roof's existing condition, construction, and expected snow loads.

Regular inspections and early repairs can help homeowners catch developing problems before winter weather makes them harder to address.

Prevent Roof Collapse from Snow and Ice This Winter features insights from Michael Majeski, a roofing expert in Fulton, New York, in HelloNation.

Michael Majeski, roofing expert in Fulton, New York, explains that excessive snow weight can strain roof structures. Wet snow and ice accumulation are especially concerning when loads exceed structural capacity.

What Are the Warning Signs of Excessive Snow Load?

According to Michael Majeski, homeowners should watch for sagging roof sections, cracked ceilings, and new leaks after snowfall. These conditions warrant prompt professional evaluation.

How Can Homeowners Reduce Ice Dam Formation?

Michael Majeski emphasizes attic insulation and ventilation as important preventive measures. More consistent roof temperatures can help limit the melt-and-refreeze cycle.

The article advises using appropriate roof rakes from the ground when safe. Michael Majeski cautions against walking on icy roofs because of fall risks and potential roofing damage.

#5563. Three charged with using AI to impersonate executives and steal $129 million

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Prosecutors say the group posed as CEOs and law firm attorneys to trick employees into wiring money; extradition requests are pending

Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit are accused of using AI to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys and steal more than $129 million from companies worldwide, U.S. prosecutors said.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York unsealed an indictment against the three foreign nationals. Soall, 41, is from Marbella, Spain, and the U.K. Hazan, 54, is from Israel. Sheetrit, 42, is from Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

Soall was arrested in Spain on June 17, Hazan was arrested in Spain on Aug. 5, and Sheetrit was arrested in the U.K. on Sept. 7. Extradition requests for all three are pending, the office said.

Between 2024 and 2026, the defendants and their co-conspirators used AI to copy how top company officials sounded or looked, and did the same for lawyers from prominent law firms, according to the indictment. They posed as CEOs and asked employees to assist with a financial transaction that had to be kept confidential. They then referred the employees to lawyers from big multinational firms, and those lawyers were impersonated too. A person posing as one of those lawyers told the employee to send a big payment by wire to an account the conspiracy controlled.

After the transfer went through, the group changed the funds into cryptocurrency to hide where they came from, then divided them up among its members, the office said. The accounts were located in the United States, Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China.

Victims included a Missouri hospital system, which lost $4,829,580, and a Rhode Island bank, which lost $2,684,580. A California hospital system lost $2,968,497, and a U.K. financial technology company lost $11,578,474. A Massachusetts mutual fund company lost $4,639,918, and a Florida pet food company lost $5,242,747.

Soall mainly impersonated U.K. attorneys and kept a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call," the office said. Hazan and Sheetrit laundered proceeds. Hazan bragged of laundering more than $400 million during the previous three years, according to the indictment.

Each defendant faces seven counts, covering a wire fraud conspiracy, substantive wire fraud, two aggravated identity theft counts, a money laundering conspiracy and two substantive money laundering counts. Each charge carries up to 20 years in prison, with the exception of aggravated identity theft, which has a ceiling of two years. Hazan was convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in 2008.

The office's release calls the technology super intelligence, a term that is the White House's preferred label for AI, according to NBC News.

"I encourage individuals and the business community to consider how to best protect themselves from the emerging threat of SI-enabled crime," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement.

FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. said in a statement that the FBI “remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities.”

The charges are accusations, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty, the office said.

#5562. ‘You’re the Bacon’: A blunt warning to Realtors about AI

NAR reports 23% of agents use AI daily and 25% weekly, while 12% do not use it and do not plan to. NAR’s Mike Woodward highlighted risks tied to free tier data use, hallucinations, and potential misrepresentation from AI edited listing photos.  AI Summary

More and more real estate professionals are turning to AI tools to automate rote tasks, manage their client relationship management systems and generate marketing collateral.

According to the National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) 2026 Realtors Technology Report released in September, nearly half of agents now use AI daily (23%) or weekly (25%), while 31% are experimenting occasionally. Only 12% said they are not using AI and do not plan to, down from 32% who had not yet tried AI in 2025.

And while AI may help agents save time or create more sophisticated looking marketing, as Mike Woodward, NAR’s director of data science, put it, quoting Spider Man “With great power, comes great responsibility.”

In a session at NAR’s 2026 NXT conference on Sunday, Woodward explored what AI can do for real estate professionals and the housing industry, as well as what it could do to agents and the industry if not used without proper caution and guardrails.

Woodward began by exploring the business model used by AI companies, because, he argues, you cannot understand the risk until you understand how AI companies make their money.

“There ain’t no such thing as a free lunch,” he says, before reaching for a darker metaphor. Two pigs in a barn admire the free shelter and the great food — right up until breakfast. “For those of you who had bacon this morning, you know how that story ends. You’re the bacon.”

As he put it, large language models are “voracious beasts” for data. Feed a free service your documents and it can ingest them, learn from them and surface what it learned to the next user.

Due to this, for anything real or confidential, pay for the service and tick the data-retention opt-out boxes, which stop the model from keeping or training on your inputs.

If the business model is the first trap, the overconfidence of LLMs is the second. Woodward warns against treating AI like “the Oracle of Delphi” — gods walking among us, dispensing truth.

To prove the point, he ran the same kinds of queries his clients run. He asked Copilot about supermarkets and schools near a Massachusetts town; it took the question too literally, omitting stores and schools in neighbouring towns. He asked Claude to pull up records for his home and five of the seven facts came back wrong.

The lesson for agents, he said, is less about the errors themselves and more about their clients.

Buyers now arrive armed with AI-generated impressions of a town or a property and it is in the agent’s interest to know what those buyers think they know.

Woodward also sought to dispel the belief that one AI model is better than the others, noting that agents need to simply pick out and learn how to make it work for them and their business. In addition to this, he also noted that there were no fancy tricks for prompting, instructing agents to “talk to it like a child”: short sentences, simple words, clear instructions.

But AI isn’t all just doomsday scenarios, according to Woodward, who noted that there were many low-risk and genuinely valuable use cases.

Some of these uses included asking Claude to create a plain-English summary of soil-analysis report and provide a step-by-step plan to fix the issues. He also used AI to create a listing description from a property fact sheet, a task that he said might take an agent 15 minutes, but done in seconds instead.

Additional applications he feels are low-risk include using AI to research companies, build charts and generate presentations that real estate professionals can use as a jumping off point.

The caveat running through all of it: on free tiers, use dummy data, and never feed in anything confidential. A performance review he rewrote for a fictional ex–Air Force employee was his cautionary tale — exactly the kind of sensitive, personal text that should never go near a free or overseas-based model.

Fixing technical faults like exposure, white balance or a tilted horizon are things industry professionals have long done using tools like photoshop. But corrections like these are now accessible to everyone thanks to AI regardless of their proficiency with photoshop.

Corrections like these, according to Woodward are fine, but removing temporary blemishes or even inventing property features like adding a fireplace, moving a window or dropping in a swimming pool can cross firmly into misrepresentation, a breach of the Realtor Code of Ethics.

But even when making image corrections, Woodward warned that sometimes the AI will make changes you never ask for.

That is the real hazard, he argues, especially given that the image goes out under the agent’s name.

“You are responsible,” he said. “You cannot say the dog ate my homework.”

The backlash, he warns, is already here: a recent front-page New York Times article in which real estate professionals “did not look good,” and pages of angry posts on Reddit. State legislatures and New York City are weighing regulation. And AI-detection tools, he believes, work well.

“If you use AI and you don’t confess to it, you’re going to get caught,” he said. “People are going to get sued for what I’m going to show you. Consumers are white-hot angry.”

But there is a legitimate version of all this, which Woodward said his lawyers were the ones to note: showing a buyer how a property could look. Virtual staging can turn an empty rental’s “prison cell” walls into something welcoming. The condition is disclosure, noting that agents should show the original alongside the edited image and label the edit clearly as AI-generated.

For Woodward one of the most important takeaways for agents is that they should pay for the tools they want to use when working with confidential information. In addition he said they should reread the code of ethics, ensure they understand the laws coming to their state and when uncertain consult with their legal counsel.

#5561. PNC Bank Launches Incoming Stablecoin Payments for Corporate and Institutional Banking Clients

Solution expands PNC's relationship with Coinbase and explores faster, more efficient payment options for corporate clients.

PITTSBURGH, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- PNC Bank today announced it is making incoming USDC payments available to PNC Corporate & Institutional Banking (C&IB) clients. Clients can receive payments in USDC, a U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin, on the Ethereum blockchain, powered by Coinbase Payment products. The solution builds on PNC's existing relationship with Coinbase and the bank's continued investment in its Treasury Management capabilities. This addition complements PNC's established faster payments capabilities and reflects the bank's ongoing focus on responding to evolving client needs with a broad range of immediate payment options.

The launch enables clients to receive USDC payments, which are automatically converted 1-to-1 to U.S. dollars and deposited into a designated PNC deposit account. The solution is designed to help businesses leverage the benefits of stablecoin payments, including faster access to funds and greater efficiency for cross-border transactions, while maintaining access to PNC's banking services.

"Our clients are continually looking at new ways to interact and transact with customers, suppliers and business partners," said Tom Lang, head of Treasury Management Product and Operations at PNC Bank. "This solution gives us an opportunity to support our customers with innovative capabilities, backed by the banking experience, risk management and expertise clients expect from PNC."

"Stablecoins are modernizing how businesses move money by making payments faster, more efficient and more global," said Alec Lovett, head of Infrastructure Products at Coinbase. "Our work with PNC shows how leading banks and trusted digital asset infrastructure come together to let corporate clients take advantage of this technology."

PNC is initially offering the service on a limited basis to eligible clients as part of a pilot program. As the use of stablecoins continues to evolve, PNC is focused on helping clients understand and evaluate emerging payment technologies and how they may fit within their broader treasury strategies.

#5560. AWS commits $100M in AI and cloud credits to health groups in underserved communities

Amazon Web Services Inc. today committed $100 million worth of artificial intelligence and cloud technology over five years to health organizations working in underserved communities around the world, provided to recipients as AWS credits.

The new AWS Health Impact Initiative is taking aim at a cost problem that AWS says is keeping many of those organizations out of the current wave of AI adoption. AWS points to survey data to explain the focus on credits.

An independent survey of 83 of the more than 400 organizations supported under the company’s earlier AWS Health Equity Initiative found that 60% saw cost as the main barrier to cloud adoption where they operate. Most ranked AWS credits as their highest-priority need. That program began in 2021 with $40 million behind it, and the total had grown to $60 million by the time the last of it was handed out in July 2024.

Timing matters too. A World Economic Forum forecast cited by AWS has generative AI use climbing faster in health care than in any other field. If the organizations closest to underserved patients fall behind on adopting it, AWS argues, health gaps will widen.

Agents and AI are reshaping health services, said Dr. Rowland Illing, chief medical officer and director of health care and life sciences at AWS, and they “too often don’t reach the communities that need them most.” Illing framed the initiative as an extension of the company’s stated aim of democratizing AI and cloud-based health technology.

Any area of health care is eligible, and AWS has singled out three for added weight. The first is access to health services, where AWS wants to support diagnostic testing and stronger health infrastructure in places such as rural areas and low- and middle-income countries.

A second area covers research into women’s and children’s health, with better data and more inclusive studies as the goal. Women’s health draws just 5% of health research funding, the company said, and as many as half the medicines given to children lack pediatric clinical validation.

Healthy food is the third area. AWS said malnutrition among pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and adolescent girls has climbed 25% since 2020 in the 12 countries hit hardest by the global food and nutrition crisis. Projects there could improve food distribution or predict food security patterns.

Recipients AWS highlighted include women’s health data nonprofit Eve’s Ark, which collects research datasets that are at risk of disappearing when a lab closes or a grant ends. Co-founder and Chief Executive Melissa Antal Iftimie said the group started with a small AWS award and “a single at-risk dataset.” The archive now holds more than a petabyte of women’s health data on AWS, and the group is building a secure research environment where scientists can work with it.

In Haiti, primary care provider Care 2 Communities runs a network of community clinics that has served 350,000 people and handles almost 120,000 patient visits a year. Its electronic medical records sit on AWS, which brings centralized, real-time data to clinics in rural parts of the country. School meals for more than 2.35 million children in India come out of kitchens run by the Akshaya Patra Foundation every school day, and the foundation uses AWS to run those kitchens and get meals out to schools.

Eligibility runs well past health charities to government agencies, research institutions and companies, and AWS will consider a project at any stage up to full production.

Organizations with an AWS account team can submit proposals through it, and a public portal is open to everyone else. Each application has to estimate how many lives the project will improve, and AWS goes through submissions every week. Successful applicants receive credits sized to their own AWS Pricing Calculator estimate of what a project needs, or a starting allocation of up to $10,000. Awardees have 12 months to use the credits and can ask to have that window stretched to 24.

#5559. The housing laws that could derail a sale — and why Realtors need to pay attention

At NAR NXT 2026, industry speakers said DSA-aligned housing policies are influencing local tenant laws. They highlighted tenant right of first refusal, just cause eviction rules, and source of income protections as issues affecting rentals, investors, and some mortgage underwriting.  AI Summary

This past week’s midterm elections saw over 100 candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) win their respective races at the federal, state, county and municipal level. While the National Association of Realtors (NAR) does not solely support one political party, instead endorsing candidates that support housing policy positions that align with NAR’s goals, Realtors are raising the alarm when it comes to some of the policies being enacted by elected DSA lawmakers.

“I am Chicken Little and I’m here to tell you that the sky is falling. But it is our responsibility to lift it up and make sure we’re aware of what’s going on so that we’re prepared,” Stacey Johnson-Cosby, an agent at ReeceNichols, a RealTrends Verified firm, said at a session during NAR’s 2026 NXT conference on Sunday. “In 40 years in the business, I’m seeing stuff now — laws and regulations that I would never have imagined and to this day can’t imagine that they’re in our marketplaces today.”

As Johnson-Cosby noted, the DSA does not believe in private property rights. Instead the group believes that housing is a human right and that properties should be owned by either the government or non-profit organizations.

“Their North Star is true social housing — housing that’s backed by public dollars. They feel housing is a human right and they’re going to make sure there is housing for everyone, whether you can afford it or not,” Johnson-Cosby said.

The things the DSA is advocating for beyond social housing, include universal rent control, tenants right to counsel and tenant organizations to organize things like rent strikes.

“Their goal is to end land and real estate speculation and decommodify housing — housing should not be for sale,” Johnson-Crosby said. “Anybody in here agree with that?”

Ending private property rights in America would not only be a drastic change for the U.S. economy, but it would also be a massive disruption to real estate and housing professionals nationwide, who are in the business of helping consumers buy and sell homes.

“They want to get rid of the concept of the white picket fence. To us, that’s the American dream. And we need the white picket fence for our clients to build wealth,” Johnson-Crosby said. “That’s our business.”

As of right now, things have not progressed this far, but Johnson-Crosby and Monica Gilroy, a founding member and managing partner at Gilroy Law Firm, said that where they are seeing an impact from DSA lawmakers and advocates is in the investor and rentals space.

Over the past decade Gilroy and Johnson-Crosby said they have seen the rise of what have been termed “tenant protection laws,” a term Johnson-Crosby does not love.

“I’m going to push back against the term tenant protection laws if the tenants are our customers. Nobody will protect our customers better than we will, right?” Johnson-Crosby, who is also a property manager, said. “We don’t need laws and elected officials and all of these groups to come in and protect our customers from us. We need them as much as they need us. We’re two sides of the same coin.”

Some of these tenant protection laws include rent control, source of income protections, just cause eviction rules, eviction moratoriums, tenant right to counsel, tenant right of first refusal and tenant bill of rights.

“These are the laws that are coming. If they’re not in your neighborhood or your jurisdiction or your city now, at some point the goal is that they would be,” Johnson-Crosby said, noting that it is important for not only property managers, but also Realtors to be aware of them if they are working with clients looking to buy or sell an investment property. “They’re spreading across the country.”

The laws Johnson-Crosby and Gilroy said agents and property managers should be most concerned about are tenant right of first refusal, just cause eviction rules and source of income protections.

Under a tenant right of first refusal, if a landlord wishes to sell a property, they must first provide the tenant with the option to purchase the home.

“Every real estate agent needs to know this. If your property that you’re listing has a renter in it, in some jurisdictions, you have to check with the renter first and give them the opportunity to determine if they’re going to buy the property,” Johnson-Crosby said. “It could be 30 days. It could be 90 days. It could be six months. It depends where they’re holding up the ability to put that house on the market until they determine if they can buy it and in some cases, they can sell the rights to a nonprofit. If this is in your marketplace, you need to know that so that your clients won’t put a house on the market, skip the tenant and end up losing money.”

With just cause evictions, renters are allowed to stay in a property as long as they want.

“If they’re not violating the law or the lease, you can’t remove them,” Johnson-Crosby said. “They are in your property for as long as they want, in perpetuity.”

If an agent is working with an investor, Johnson-Crosby and Gilroy said they need to be aware of these laws, so their client knows the risks they may be facing in venturing into this business.

While these laws can certainly have an impact, the one Johnson-Crosby and Gilroy said agents need to be especially aware of is source of income protection. In some jurisdictions, source of income has become a protected class under fair housing laws, meaning that a person cannot be denied housing based on their source of income, which may be alimony, gig work, rental assistance programs or a housing choice voucher. The denial of housing due to source of income has become the subject of multiple lawsuits over the past few years tied to rentals, but this is also a concern for lenders as it is pushing into the mortgage space when looking at someone’s ability to obtain a mortgage.

“Fair Housing is obviously something that is crucially important in our industry and we want to always be sure we’re doing everything we can to stay as compliant as possible with it,” Gilroy said.

While many of these laws are currently happening at the local level, Johnson-Crosby and Gilroy said agents need to keep an eye on these things as they may be coming to their market next.

“This is going on throughout the United States, and one of the worst things that can happen — it spreads to other states. If it happens at a national level, you’re going to be impacted,” Johnson-Crosby said. “And it can happen at the White House through regulatory agencies.”

This is why Johnson-Crosby said Realtor members need to be in contact with their local, state and federal lawmakers.

“If [lawmakers] want to create more housing, have us at the table so we can tell you what really works — from the people who actually create the housing,” Johnson-Crosby said. “We met with the state reps and we got a law put into place that pre-empted source of income in our state and we killed it through advocacy.”

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is trading near $1.30 as institutional demand and tightening supply return to the spotlight. Standard Chartered still sees XRP price reaching $28 despite cutting its near-term prediction.

The bank’s target would require XRP to climb more than 2,000% from current levels. That makes institutional adoption and sustained buying pressure central to the bullish case.

U.S. spot XRP ETFs have accumulated 1.2 billion XRP since launching. Meanwhile, Ripple’s escrow system continues releasing tokens, creating a potential clash between institutional demand and available supply.

Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick lowered his 2026 XRP price target to $2.80 earlier this year. However, the bank maintained its long-term forecast of $28 by 2030. Kendrick’s bullish thesis relies on institutional participation, regulatory clarity, and greater use of blockchain payment infrastructure. Spot ETFs provide one potential route for traditional investors to gain exposure.

The question now is whether those products can absorb enough XRP to influence market supply.

That dynamic could amplify price movements during periods of rising demand. A genuine supply shock would require persistent buying to overwhelm available sellers across exchanges and other markets.

Ripple’s escrow system adds another layer to the XRP price prediction. The company releases up to one billion XRP from escrow each month, with unused tokens often returned to new escrow contracts. Ripple is reportedly holding 31.7 billion XRP in escrow. Its total XRP holdings stood at 36.8 billion.

But could XRP touch $28? The bullish scenario would require ETF purchases and institutional accumulation to outpace selling pressure. Greater use of XRP in payments and tokenized financial markets could provide additional demand.

XRP price remains far below Standard Chartered’s long-term prediction, for now. The token’s ability to hold recent support and attract renewed ETF inflows will help determine the supply-squeeze thesis and whether it can gain traction.

A sustained institutional buying cycle could strengthen the case for a much larger rally. Reaching $28, however, would require years of adoption growth beyond the ETF market alone.

#5555. Hedge funds sold tech stocks at a near-record pace after midterm elections

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Gross leverage at U.S. fundamental long-short funds fell 8.7 percentage points to 207.5%, the biggest weekly drop since March 2020

Hedge funds unloaded global tech shares last week at a rate that nearly matched the record in Goldman Sachs $GS figures dating to 2016, according to Bloomberg.

Tech saw more net selling than any other sector, both worldwide and in the U.S., according to Bloomberg. The selling produced the largest surge in net sales of individual equities in four months, based on Goldman's prime brokerage figures through Nov. 6. Hedge funds also offloaded American industrial shares faster than at any point since April 2020.

Investors cut risk after the U.S. midterm elections prompted doubts over how fast data centers would be built and how much chip and other infrastructure demand would follow, according to Bloomberg.

Gross leverage at U.S. fundamental long-short funds shrank by 8.7 percentage points to 207.5%, a weekly drop not exceeded since March 2020, Bloomberg said. Net leverage fell by 3.7 percentage points to reach 43.3%, its steepest one-week drop since the week of “Liberation Day” in April 2025.

Selling eased by the end of the week. Hedge funds ended the week as net purchasers in figures from Goldman's equity trading desk, lifted by Friday buying, according to Bloomberg. A large part of that buying reflected short covering in macro trades involving indexes and ETFs.

Tech stocks dropped sharply on Nov. 5. Nvidia $NVDA stock fell 9.3%, AMD $AMD stock fell 17.3%, Micron $MU stock fell 17.5%, Broadcom $AVGO stock fell 10.4% and Microsoft $MSFT stock fell 3.6%. CoreWeave stock fell 10%.

Dozens of municipal-level ballot proposals across 10 states, each aimed at limiting data-center construction, went to voters on Nov. 3, according to CNBC. Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, wrote in a note that investors were assessing what a Democrat-controlled Congress could mean for technology oversight and the AI boom, according to CNBC.

Hedge funds had already been reducing AI exposure. They posted their worst monthly performance relative to the S&P 500 in more than two decades in July as popular AI positions unwound. Goldman strategists led by Ben Snider said July marked one of the sharpest hedge fund de-grossing episodes of the past decade.

#5554. Longbridge promotes Melissa Macerato to president and chief commercial officer

Longbridge Financial promoted longtime executive Melissa Macerato to president and chief commercial officer, recognizing her role in building sales, marketing, training and product development as the company expanded beyond reverse mortgages into broader home equity solutions for homeowners 55 and older.   AI Summary

Melissa Macerato has been promoted to president and chief commercial officer at Longbridge Financial, moving up from her prior role as chief revenue and marketing officer, the company announced Monday.

Macerato has been a key member of the company’s leadership team since 2012, helping guide its evolution from an emerging reverse mortgage lender into a broader home equity lender serving homeowners 55 and older, according to the company announcement.

Longbridge reported a 31% market share and annualized growth exceeding 40% since January 2024 in its core business of serving older homeowners. The company said Macerato’s promotion recognizes more than a decade of contributions to its business strategy, organizational development and culture.

“Melissa has represented the heart and soul of Longbridge since joining us during our startup phase, when we didn’t have a single loan officer. She led the development of our entire sales, marketing, and training departments, which together now account for more than 40% of our employees,” CEO Chris Mayer said in a statement.

“Over the years, Longbridge’s sales team has reached new highs in productivity, even amid the challenges of a high-interest-rate environment. Under Melissa’s leadership, Longbridge has achieved and maintained its No. 1 position as the industry’s largest third-party originator, with continued gains in volume and market share and a deep commitment to helping our partners grow their businesses. Equally important, she has been instrumental in building our unique culture, where 94% of employees say Longbridge is a great place to work,” Mayer said.

Throughout her tenure, Macerato has overseen sales, training, marketing and human resources, along with Longbridge’s product development division. The company said she has been responsible for building teams and infrastructure to support Longbridge’s expansion and diversification.

Working with Mayer and the executive leadership team, Macerato helped take HELOC For Seniors, a home equity line of credit for borrowers 62 and older, from concept to market. She has also helped grow Longbridge’s proprietary Platinum reverse mortgage portfolio, supporting the shift toward a broader mix of home equity products.

Macerato brings more than 20 years of leadership experience across banking, mortgage lending and financial services. She began her career at MBNA America as a vice president before joining GE Capital as a senior director. At GE Capital, she was selected as one of the original participants in its Six Sigma quality process management program and achieved Black Belt status.

She later joined MetLife, where she eventually led reverse mortgage sales. There, she hired more than 150 salespeople and managers, helping to establish the company as a major reverse mortgage lender. After MetLife began winding down its bank, she joined Longbridge in 2012, a few months after the lender’s founding.

In her expanded role, Macerato will help lead Longbridge’s next phase of growth and oversee the rollout of new products and tools designed to help borrowers 55 and older understand how home equity can fit into a retirement strategy. For lenders and brokers working in the senior housing market, the company’s focus on new product suites and education tools could broaden partnerships and add options for borrowers who may not fit traditional reverse mortgage profiles.

#5552. Diagrid’s Dapr 1.19 lightens AI agent workflows and drops a control-plane service

Agent infrastructure startup Diagrid Inc. today released Dapr 1.19 with changes that cut the overhead of the durable workflows behind long-running artificial intelligence agents.

Operators of the open-source runtime can also drop one of its control-plane services. Until 1.19, Dapr’s workflow engine shipped the entire execution history to the worker on every step.

Each one adds to that history. On a job that runs for hours or fans out into dozens of parallel tasks, the payload keeps growing, and Diagrid said that pushed up latency and memory use. Now a worker keeps what it already holds and gets only new events.

That makes the data sent per step independent of how long a workflow has been running. Workers still replay the full history locally. The smaller transfers go only to workers that advertise support for them, which in 1.19 means those built on Dapr’s Java and Python software development kits.

Mark Fussell, Diagrid’s co-founder and chief product officer, said an agent “that runs all afternoon and splits into 50 tasks can’t haul its entire history across the network on every step.”

A second workflow change, an opt-in preview feature called WorkflowsFastPath, stops pushing every workflow event through a durable scheduler reminder. Wake-ups and local activities are handled in place. The reminder path stays as a backstop for recovery, and in Diagrid’s engine benchmarks median step latency fell from 553 milliseconds to 153 milliseconds with the feature on.

Two services have made up Dapr’s control plane until now, and a new mode in 1.19 retires Placement, which distributes the actor placement table. The surviving Scheduler service handles jobs, reminders and workflow scheduling, and it already tracks cluster membership and pushes state to sidecars the same way Placement does.

Yaron Schneider, a co-creator of Dapr who is also Diagrid’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said the pair “matured as two services doing overlapping work.” With the mode on, the Scheduler takes over actor placement and the standalone Placement service is no longer deployed. That spares operators a stateful service and the Raft consensus cluster behind it. Reminders get faster too, because the Scheduler knows which sidecar owns each actor.

Scaling events are also less disruptive. A host joining or leaving used to pause placement across the entire namespace while Dapr re-sent its placement table. In the new mode, only the affected actor types are locked and updated, and the rest keep serving traffic.

New alpha building blocks in 1.19 are aimed at developers of AI applications. A Vector building block offers a portable application programming interface for storing and querying embeddings through similarity search, with Meilisearch as its first supported component.

Binary Store streams large files such as model outputs in chunks so they never have to sit in memory whole. Its first components cover Amazon S3 and the object stores from Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle.

Developers working in .NET get Actors.Next, a new actor SDK that generates proxies and registration code at compile time, which cuts runtime overhead and lets actor apps compile with Native AOT.

Dapr 1.19 is available now. WorkflowsFastPath ships turned off, and the Scheduler placement mode is enabled through a Helm setting once every sidecar runs 1.19, with no sidecar restart needed to switch it on or off. Teams running Dapr on Kubernetes can manage the upgrade through Diagrid’s Dapr Ops Dashboard, and the company said the tool typically supports new releases within 24 hours.

#5551. E.U. ministers are pushing for a December deal on ECB's next president

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Finance ministers took stock of nominations from Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos as leaders weigh filling three ECB jobs as one package

Euro zone finance ministers reviewed two candidacies to succeed European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde on Monday and passed the matter to EU leaders, who are aiming to settle it in December, according to Bloomberg.

Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis said in a statement that the group received two candidacies by the Nov. 6 deadline: Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands. Lagarde will resign by Feb. 7, 2027, the Eurogroup said.

“It is possible that all three appointments will be considered together at the level of European leaders in order to facilitate consensus,” Pierrakakis told reporters in Brussels on Monday, according to Bloomberg. Before the meeting, he told reporters it would be mainly an information point and a discussion, because leaders have traditionally driven the decision, according to RTÉ.

Leaders also have to fill the seats held by Isabel Schnabel, who oversees market operations, and Chief Economist Philip Lane. Officials said the three jobs are likely to be negotiated as a package among France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands, according to RTÉ.

Knot is a former Dutch central bank governor, and Hernández de Cos heads the Bank for International Settlements, according to RTÉ.

Under the process the Eurogroup described, the European Council appoints ECB Executive Board members on a recommendation from the Council. That recommendation needs a reinforced qualified majority: at least 16 of the 21 euro area countries, representing at least 65% of the euro area population. The ECB and the European Parliament are consulted before the European Council makes a final decision.

Leaders may take up the issue as early as Friday, when they gather informally in Dublin, according to Bloomberg. Meetings are also scheduled for Nov. 26-27 and Dec. 17-18 in Brussels, Bloomberg said.

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen said the pick should turn on merit rather than on political horse-trading, according to RTÉ. Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo voiced optimism that Hernández de Cos will get the job, according to RTÉ.

Lagarde announced on Oct. 29 that she would step down before her term ends. Schnabel is leaving on Jan. 3 to join the International Monetary Fund, and Lane's term ends May 31.

#5550. Massachusetts voters narrowly reject minimum lot size measure

Massachusetts voters narrowly rejected Question 7, a first of its kind ballot initiative that would have limited local zoning barriers for qualifying single family lots. Supporters say the results highlight voter confusion and potential targets for future zoning reform, including Boston.  AI Summary

Massachusetts voters narrowly rejected a ballot measure last week that would have forced towns and cities to allow single-family homes on smaller home sites than most local zoning rules currently permit.

The vote on the first-of-its-kind ballot initiative nationwide was so close that the Associated Press called the race only on Friday, nearly three days after the election. It was the last ballot question decided because the gap, roughly 32,000 votes, was the smallest margin among the nine questions on the ballot.

Local government organizations fought the measure, arguing it was a top-down approach that limited local control over zoning. Municipalities have made that argument against any reform that includes preemption, winning some fights and losing others.

In a statement after the AP projection, Massachusetts Municipal Association Executive Director and CEO Adam Chapdelaine thanked voters for “recognizing that Question 7 was not an effective or workable approach to creating entry-level homes in the Commonwealth.”

Still, supporters are treating the close result as a win.

“If you told me six years ago that we would have a statewide ballot to change zoning statewide across the entire Commonwealth, and it would barely lose within one percentage point, I would have thought you were crazy,” Jonathan Berk, board chair of six-year-old Abundant Housing Massachusetts, told HousingWire TBD.

The measure would have required “that cities and towns allow single-family homes on residentially zoned lots that meet minimum standards of at least 5,000 square feet in area, at least 50 feet of frontage on a street or public way, and access to public sewer and water services.” In effect, the state law would preempt local zoning rules that require single-family home lots to be larger than 5,000 square feet, which is about 0.12 acres. Cities and towns could still have set reasonable rules on setbacks, height, bulk, and short-term rentals.

Supporters said the change would spur starter-home construction and make ownership more attainable for working- and middle-class families since many localities currently zone for a minimum single-family lot area of one-half to two acres.

While the result disappointed proponents, it gave them valuable information on where to press for smaller lot sizes.

Voters in Boston overwhelmingly supported smaller lot sizes even though the city was exempt from the measure. Rural communities on well water and septic systems were also outside the measure’s reach but voted against it.

Berk said the outcome points to confusion among voters in both groups. Rural voters did not understand that the measure did not apply to them.

“I would bet that a lot of those voters thought they were voting for something that applied to Boston,” he said.

Berk said the city is missing an opportunity, adding that Mayor Michelle Wu has been “a bit gun shy” about large-scale zoning reform. He said Boston’s zoning code is the longest in the country, about four times the length of New York City’s, and that 99% of the city’s residential land is “existing non-conforming.”

Boston is one of the least affordable big cities in the country. HousingWire Intelligence shows median monthly rent at $3,900, on par with San Francisco and New York City. A median home list price of $890,000 puts Boston in competition with California cities.

A knock against Boston is that building in the city is expensive because of zoning code challenges.

“It’s hard to develop here. It should be,” Boston Planning Chief Kairos Shen said during an October inclusionary zoning symposium on housing costs sponsored by the MIT Center for Real Estate.

“You guys want us to lower our standards,” Shen added. “Part of my job is to hold those standards and try to still make them work.”

The forum included representatives from developers The Davis Companies and Oxford Properties.

Policies requiring income-restricted units in market-rate apartment projects have drawn broad criticism. That is one factor in stalling Boston multifamily production. Higher construction costs and interest rates have also played a role.

Rental construction is only part of the picture. The ownership side is where the ballot question and Boston’s zoning code also collide.

“I do hope that this gives some cover to Mayor Wu in Boston to actually pursue some more dramatic zoning reform in the city,” Berk said, citing single-family lot sizes and modest middle housing such as townhomes and duplexes.
