#5548. Graceful Finance’s Anna Frankowska pitches home reversions for seniors’ toolbox

Graceful Finance founder and CEO Anna Frankowska is introducing a home reversion product in the U.S., starting in Florida, as an alternative to reverse mortgages and other home equity lending tools. Frankowska told HousingWire’s Reverse Mortgage Daily that financial advisers and reverse mortgage lenders are receptive, seeing it as another tool amid high rates and the lock-in effect, although regulatory treatment and capital markets appetite will shape its long-term growth.  AI Summary

Anna Frankowska, founder and CEO of Graceful Finance, is pitching home reversion products to U.S. seniors. Her company’s Lifestyle Agreement product aims to be an alternative to reverse mortgages and other home equity lending tools amid high interest rates and the lock-in effect.

“There is no loan, so no interest builds up against the home,” Frankowska said in written comments given to HousingWire’s Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD). “Pricing is driven mostly by the home’s value, how the housing market performs and life expectancy.”

Under a home reversion structure, homeowners essentially sell a share of their future ownership rights in exchange for a lump sum payment, regular income or a combination of both. They retain the right to live in the home for life without mortgage or rent payments.

The minimum age for the product is 75, higher than the 62-year minimum for Federal Housing Administration-insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) and the typical 55-plus eligibility for many proprietary reverse mortgage products.

Frankowska launched Graceful about four years ago with the goal of adapting a product more common in Europe to the U.S. market, starting in Florida. She added that reverse mortgage lenders and financial advisers have been “receptive” so far, viewing home reversion as another tool they can offer clients.

In an interview with RMD, Frankowska discussed the regulatory treatment of home reversions in the U.S., the product’s growth potential and capital markets appetite.

Editor’s note: This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Flávia Nunes: How competitive is the home equity solutions market today, given high interest rates and the mortgage rate lock-in effect?

Anna Frankowska: Many older homeowners have most of their wealth tied up in their homes, while their everyday costs keep rising. Home equity is the natural place for them to turn to supplement their income and enhance their lifestyles. However, high interest rates are putting pressure on the value of reverse mortgages, especially HECMs.

Diving a little deeper, we see it in the numbers. When rates rise, a reverse mortgage borrower can access less of their home’s value. Not surprisingly, HECM endorsements fell 14.2% year over year, from 28,172 in fiscal year 2025 to 24,182 in FY2026, reaching their lowest level since FY2003.

This creates an opportunity for products like home reversions, which are less sensitive to interest rates. There is no loan, so no interest builds up against the home. Pricing is driven mostly by the home’s value, how the housing market performs and life expectancy.

FN: How receptive have traditional reverse mortgage lenders and financial advisers been to partnering with Graceful as a referral option?

AF: Very receptive. Every person I’ve spoken with in the industry wants to help people age better. They want more tools in their toolbox, and they know there are gaps in the existing product suite. There are barriers in the reverse mortgage that are hard to overcome for some homeowners.

For example, at today’s rates, the amount a homeowner can access may simply not be enough. And income solutions are top of mind for the financial advisers I talk to. Professionals in this industry are busy with their immediate priorities and the products they know. That creates a place for us to support them with an additional option.

Our conversations with reverse mortgage lenders helped us think through what’s working and what isn’t, and who helped share what Graceful does. So we really see ourselves as an integral part of the ecosystem, working alongside reverse mortgage lenders.

FN: How has Graceful adapted its product to the U.S. market compared with the home reversion models available in other countries?

AF: We took the concepts of the European markets and adapted them to American preferences. I see it through three lenses: the legal framework, the existing products and how capital markets work.On the first two, we heard directly from customers on their needs for access to their home equity to generate income and that helped us understand what we should be solving for. Looking internationally, we imported best practices from the U.K. market, such as mandatory independent counseling, a suitability assessment, a vulnerable customer policy that classifies all elderly participants as vulnerable by default, plain-language disclosures, a trusted contact requirement, and a comparison process. The result is an attractive product design with strong consumer protections, structured within the U.S. legal framework.

To find capital to fund our home equity solutions, we draw on the U.S. capital markets, which offer deeper securitization markets than Europe’s and a broader range of funding opportunities. Investor interest in these products is high. Deep U.S. markets give us access to more capital, a wider range of investors, and more choice in how we structure our funding. Together, we expect this to support significant volume in the U.S.

FN: As Graceful looks to expand into California and Texas, what specific regulatory challenges are you navigating compared with Florida?

AF: The fundamental homeowner need remains the same across these states. Let me first mention that helping seniors age better is a bipartisan policy priority. I think this will become even more of a priority as the senior support system comes under increasing pressure.

Of course, each state has its own legal and regulatory framework, and we are approaching the expansion thoughtfully. We know that a structure developed in Florida cannot simply be replicated elsewhere. This includes, but is not limited to, state-specific real estate and consumer protection requirements, property and title law, property taxes, and ongoing ownership obligations.

However, I wouldn’t call them challenges, but rather different regulatory frameworks that we need to build into our model and supplement with our strong consumer protection mindset.

FN: How are you approaching funding and capital markets opportunities?

AF: We’re seeing a strong appetite, for a couple of reasons. Investors are looking for long-duration assets with competitive returns and cash flows they can match against long-dated liabilities, which is exactly what many insurance companies need. In addition, they like asset-backed investments with a real asset behind them. Notably, this includes the U.S. housing market, which is very large with decades of extensive and well-documented price history.

Our approach to funding is step by step. We’re starting with anchor partners who can fund the portfolio while it’s young, and building the track record and scale that larger institutions need. From there, more financing channels open up.

FN: Critics argue that selling a portion or all of a home’s future ownership can limit a homeowner’s ability to pass the property on to heirs. How are your clients and their families navigating that trade-off in practice?

AF: As we did our consumer research, we heard that a top priority for older Americans is not to be a burden on their children. Finding sources of income to balance their current lifestyles and future needs will often be more important than passing on their property.

Our focus is on helping older homeowners enjoy the wealth they’ve accumulated, which includes remaining in their houses. Except for the wealthiest, many older Americans struggle to make ends meet and have to choose between having a fulfilling retirement or leaving a legacy for their children. We are providing them that option. Certainly, if a legacy is the most important objective for someone, we would not expect them to try to access their home equity.

The practical reality is that most people have to prioritize either current lifestyle or legacy. It is our mission to make finance available to empower people to live their elder years on their own terms. It is common for something unexpected, especially with health, to occur as we age.

By setting up their home equity release early before that event, people can access some of the wealth they have built in their homes before a situation becomes a crisis, they have more options to invest in their health, home, care, transportation and overall quality of life.

FN: What do you see as the home reversion product’s long-term growth potential in the U.S.?

AF: We believe in building a foundation for the long term. As we build growth, our early focus will be on client experience, ease of doing business, product refinement and deep relationships. Over the last couple of months, we have been focused on product iterations and listening to the market. To give you an early preview, that work has led us to expand our offering, which isn’t live yet.

The time for rapid growth will come because demand is growing. But getting this right is extremely important, so right now we are focused on our home market in Florida, with California and Texas next. Long term, I see a future where people have multiple options that work for them, with reverse mortgages sitting side by side with home reversions, among others.

To put it simply, it’s a multibillion-dollar annual volume opportunity. For scale, homeowners 62 and older hold $15.34 trillion in home equity, and the entire reverse mortgage industry originated about $7.3 billion last year. That’s less than a tenth of one percent of that equity converted each year.

When people are young, they dream of owning a home as a place to raise a family, enjoy time with friends and grow old. It is also one of the best ways to accumulate wealth. In order to enjoy that wealth as they grow old and live the life they desire, home equity release serves an important role.

#5547. Little Giant is recalling 3.6 million ladders over a fall hazard that caused head injuries

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The recall covers 11 models sold from December 2015 through October 2026, with 19 injuries reported to the company

Little Giant Ladder Systems is recalling about 3.7 million ladders that can retract if their Rapid Locks are not engaged, a fall hazard tied to reports of head injuries, according to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. The agency’s notice says the ladders “can suddenly retract if the Rapid Locks are not fully engaged.”

Little Giant, based in Springville, Utah, said it has been notified of 25 incidents in which the ladders retracted, and 19 of them involved injuries. Three involved harm to the head, from skull fractures and concussions to traumatic brain injury, along with lost vision, lost hearing and cognitive impairment. The other 16 ranged from bruises and cuts to broken bones and fractured joints. The company has also logged 39 complaints that the Rapid Locks malfunctioned.

Rapid Locks insert into ladder rungs to adjust the ladder's height. They are black or orange and sit on each ladder leg.

The recall covers these models: Adjustable Fortress 2.0, Conquest 2.0, Dark Horse 2.0, Epic, King Kombo XT, Leveler, MegaLite, MegaLite+, Multi, Quantum and Vector. Only ladders without an orange rectangular "QC" sticker on the rail above one of the Rapid Locks are included.

The ladders were sold at Lowe's $LOW, Costco $COST and other stores, and online at Lowes.com, Amazon $AMZN.com, Costco.com, LittleGiantLadders.com and other websites, from December 2015 through October 2026. Prices ranged from about $100 to $1,000. The ladders were made in the United States, China, Mexico and Malaysia.

Consumers should stop using the recalled ladders until they review the information at littlegiantladders.com/pages/recalls or through the QR code on the ladder. They should then contact Little Giant for a repair kit with warning labels and instructions. The labels advise users to verify that the Rapid Locks are engaged before every use and to maintain the locks with lubrication.

Consumers whose Rapid Lock does not function after lubrication should contact Little Giant for evaluation. If a lock still fails after that evaluation, the company will provide either a replacement ladder matching the original model or a comparable one, or a refund. Refunds are prorated for depreciation according to when the ladder was bought, but they cover the full price for purchases made in the last year.

Little Giant posted the CPSC notice, released Nov. 5, on its website. The company is also providing repair kits to every known user who reported Rapid Lock malfunctions, according to Fox Business. Consumers can reach Little Giant toll-free at 866-201-9069.

#5545. Burger King is bringing back its miniature restaurant advent calendar for a third year

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The 12-door calendar costs $19.54, with 110 available each day from Nov. 16 through Nov. 20 on BKAdventCalendar.com

Burger King is bringing back its advent calendar for a third year, with 12 miniature pieces that assemble into a model Burger King restaurant, the company said. The 2026 calendar will be available starting Nov. 16 at $19.54, a figure that nods to the chain's founding year.

Each of the calendar’s 12 doors holds a miniature piece, the company said. The items include a Whopper in its new box packaging, nuggets, the King’s Booth, a soda fountain, a reindeer and a holiday tree. On the 12th day, the pieces fit together as a finished tiny Burger King restaurant. The final door also yields a pint-sized $5 digital coupon that Royal Perks members can redeem.

“We know Guests will be excited that for the third year in a row, the Advent Calendar is back,” Joel Yashinsky, chief marketing officer of Burger King U.S. and Canada, said in a statement.

Burger King will make 110 calendars available at noon ET on each of five days, from Monday, Nov. 16, to Friday, Nov. 20, or until inventory runs out, the company said. BKAdventCalendar.com is the sole sales channel. That schedule totals 550 calendars nationwide, according to Attractions Magazine.

Each order, household, address, name and email address is limited to one calendar, the company said. Shipping is free and standard to the 48 contiguous states and Washington, D.C., excluding Alaska, Hawaii, U.S. territories and P.O. boxes. Calendars are scheduled to ship the week of Nov. 30.

Burger King said each of its past two calendars was gone within five minutes of going on sale. The 2025 version came stocked with an inflatable chair, holiday ornaments and plush toys, according to Allrecipes.

#5544. Broadcom open-sources its Kubernetes VM manager

Broadcom Inc. is contributing an open-source project for managing virtual machines with Kubernetes to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, part of an effort to simplify operations across increasingly diverse enterprise computing environments.

The company announced today that its VM application programming interface project has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, the entry point for early-stage cloud-native projects. VM API  provides a vendor-neutral framework for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same APIs that Kubernetes employs to orchestrate modular and portable software containers.

Broadcom also announced an initiative to standardize application behavior across Kubernetes distributions and expanded support for third-party software on VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service.

The announcements, made at KubeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect the growing need for infrastructure that can support traditional applications alongside modern containerized and artificial intelligence workloads.

Although Kubernetes has become the dominant platform for container orchestration, virtual machines remain central to enterprise computing. A Linux Foundation survey of 492 practitioners scheduled to be released today found that VMs account for 53% of production applications, with most respondents expecting that proportion to remain stable. Among organizations expanding their VM deployments, 34% cited AI and agentic workloads as contributing factors.

Broadcom’s VM API project addresses the operational complexity of managing VMs and containers separately. It uses Kubernetes’ declarative management model to create and manage virtual machines across different infrastructure providers while preserving capabilities such as hardware isolation and specialized input/output performance.

“We want to do the same thing now for virtual machines,” said Prashanth Shenoy, Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions, referring to Kubernetes’ existing Cluster API initiative.

The goal is to provide consistent management across environments without requiring organizations to abandon their existing virtualization investments.

“Ultimately, our goal is to make virtual machines first-class citizens of a Kubernetes environment without sacrificing what makes them distinct and valuable for our customers,” Shenoy said.

The project could also simplify operations for administrators accustomed to working with Kubernetes rather than maintaining separate management tools for virtualized and containerized infrastructure.

Broadcom’s second initiative addresses a different interoperability problem: inconsistent application behavior across Kubernetes distributions.

The company is co-chairing a newly established Workload Conformance Working Group to develop common expectations for how applications operate across Kubernetes environments.

Existing conformance programs verify that Kubernetes distributions support standard APIs, but that doesn’t guarantee applications will behave identically across platforms. Differences in infrastructure capabilities, configuration and operational practices can introduce incompatibilities.

“Just because two Kubernetes environments are conformant doesn’t necessarily mean that the application will behave consistently across both,” Shenoy said.

The proposed workload conformance standard would help software vendors reduce the need to certify applications separately for individual Kubernetes distributions while giving enterprises greater confidence in application portability.

Broadcom also announced more than 20 newly validated partner solutions for VKS, the Kubernetes runtime integrated into VMware Cloud Foundation.

The validations span observability, security, data management, AI, application delivery, networking and storage. They are intended to help organizations deploy Kubernetes workloads using familiar third-party tools without requiring extensive integration or changes to existing operational practices.

Broadcom said its broader VKS ecosystem now includes more than 90 independent software vendors participating in testing and validation.

#5543. Massumi + Consoli Expands to Silicon Valley with Former Weil Private Equity and M&A Partner Matt Stewart

New office will establish M+C's presence in a major hub for private equity, M&A and technology, building on a series of significant senior partner additions nationwide

PALO ALTO, Calif., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Massumi + Consoli ("M+C"), a nationwide law firm recognized for its leading private equity and M&A practice, today announced plans to open a new office in the Silicon Valley with the addition of private equity/M&A partner Matt Stewart. The expansion bolsters M+C's position in one of the country's most prominent legal markets.

"The caliber of partners we're attracting speaks to the strength of our platform and the opportunities ahead," said Peter Massumi, Co-Founder of Massumi + Consoli. "Matt Stewart is the most recent example. He built a leading private equity practice. He had compelling opportunities to join some of the largest firms in the country. But he chose M+C because, in his words, this is the best platform to serve his clients. That's a strong endorsement of what we've built so far and what we intend on building together."

Stewart brings more than two decades of experience advising private equity funds and strategic acquirers. He is joining M+C from Weil, Gotshal & Manges, where he advised private equity funds such as Advent International, BlackRock, Khosla Ventures, Norwest Venture Partners, TPG and Trive Capital. He has been recognized as a "Notable Practitioner" for M&A in the U.S. by IFLR1000 and a "Rising Star" for Private Equity by Law360. He has also been named to The Daily Journal's 40 Under 40 list and recognized as an Emerging Leader by The M&A Advisor.

"Expanding our presence in the Silicon Valley is a significant step for our firm and a natural extension of our private equity and M&A practice," said Anthony Consoli, Co-Founder of Massumi + Consoli. "We wanted to grow here with an exceptional lawyer who has the experience, relationships and reputation to help us build a meaningful presence. #5542. Goodyear is replacing its CEO as the struggling tire maker's stock falls

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Board director Roger Wood takes over as interim CEO while Goodyear searches for a permanent chief and continues a strategic review

Goodyear Tire & Rubber appointed director Roger Wood interim CEO on Monday, replacing CEO Mark Stewart, who stepped down as CEO and president and resigned from the board. The company said the board will search for a permanent successor with an executive search firm.

Goodyear stock slipped 3.7% to $4.20 ahead of Monday's opening bell.

"Goodyear has made meaningful progress in becoming a more efficient and focused company, and the board believes this is the right moment to transition leadership to accelerate that progress and capture additional opportunity," Board Chair Joe Hinrichs said in a statement.

Wood said his immediate priorities are to support associates and customers, sharpen execution and build on work already under way. "I look forward to working closely with the board, leadership team and the Enterprise Transformation Office to advance the strategic review," he said in a statement.

Goodyear disclosed terms of the change in a regulatory filing. Wood, 64, has been a Goodyear director since July 2023. He was co-CEO of Tenneco from 2018 to 2020 and president and CEO of Dana Holding from 2011 to 2015. He will remain a director but will leave the Human Capital and Compensation Committee and the Governance Committee during his interim tenure.

Wood will receive a salary of $310,000 per month, the filing said. He will receive a monthly restricted stock unit grant with a grant date value of $1 million for five months or until a permanent successor is hired, whichever is shorter. He also gets temporary housing, car and travel allowances.

The filing said Stewart's separation counts as a termination "other than for Cause" under the company's Executive Severance and Change in Control Plan.

A special committee of the board, formed this year, has been conducting a strategic review of Goodyear's businesses and operations. The company said the review aims to improve how the business performs and to create more value for shareholders. The board and the company are weighing steps such as fine-tuning the mix of businesses and the footprint, raising efficiency and putting money into new products and capabilities.

Goodyear said it plans no more updates unless its board concludes that further disclosure is warranted or necessary.

#5539. Red Hat adds agentic AI operations, stronger security in OpenShift 5 and RHEL updates

Red Hat Inc. today announced a major update to its OpenShift Kubernetes-based application development platform that adds artificial intelligence-powered troubleshooting, stronger security controls and simplified upgrades as the company seeks to make its hybrid cloud infrastructure easier to manage.

The company also announced new versions of Red Hat Enterprise Linux with enhanced protection against software tampering, AI-assisted system administration and post-quantum cryptography.

The releases, unveiled at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect Red Hat’s continuing initiatives to embed AI into enterprise infrastructure management while strengthening security across increasingly distributed environments.

Red Hat OpenShift 5, the first major version upgrade in seven years, extends the platform’s ability to manage containers, virtual machines and AI workloads within a common environment. It also broadens the OpenShift Lightspeed generative AI assistant into an agent capable of investigating operational problems and recommending corrective actions.

“It’s infusing intelligence into the platform with agent-based troubleshooting through a simple interface with Lightspeed and natural language,” said Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer and senior vice president of global engineering.

The updated Lightspeed interface allows administrators to generate visualizations of system performance using natural-language requests. For example, an administrator can ask for central processing unit utilization over the previous week, add memory consumption and overlay application errors. The resulting charts can be saved to dashboards that update continuously.

More significantly, OpenShift 5 introduces agentic troubleshooting that automatically investigates cluster events. When problems occur, the system can examine related information, reason through possible causes and propose remediation steps. Administrators retain control over whether the recommended actions are executed.

The platform also includes an AI-driven upgrade planner that examines application dependencies, Kubernetes application programming interfaces and optional operators to identify potential compatibility problems before updates begin.

“It is easy to upgrade Kubernetes,” said Mike Barrett, Red Hat’s vice president and general manager of hybrid cloud platforms. “What is difficult is navigating all the things you’re running on top of Kubernetes.”

Security enhancements include hardened multitenancy, more extensive network isolation, automated certificate management and post-quantum cryptography for control-plane communications. The capabilities are aimed in part at sovereign cloud providers and regulated organizations that must maintain strict separation between tenants and demonstrate compliance with security requirements.

OpenShift 5 also supports automated graphics processing unit resource allocation across AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads, potentially improving utilization of that expensive computing infrastructure.

Unlike previous major platform transitions, OpenShift 5 can be installed as an in-place update from OpenShift 4, avoiding the need to reinstall software or migrate workloads, Red Hat said. A revised lifecycle approach provides greater predictability for customers operating long-lived enterprise applications and virtualized infrastructure.

“We are no longer asking you to reinstall or migrate to use more of our product,” Barrett said. “This is a simple upgrade.”

The company is emphasizing virtualization as an increasingly important part of its business. Barrett said OpenShift Virtualization has grown to an $800 million business as customers seek alternatives to traditional virtualization platforms.

It said NASA’s laboratory migrated approximately 2,400 virtual machines to OpenShift Virtualization, while Gates Corp. moved more than 1,300 virtual machines and reported a 50% increase in available compute capacity.

The forthcoming Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.3 and 9.9 releases extend the company’s security strategy to the operating system.

A principal addition in RHEL 10.3 is support for sealed images, which use customer-controlled cryptographic keys to verify operating system integrity from the bootloader through the kernel and root file system. The technology is designed to prevent unauthorized modifications and block compromised software components from running.

Red Hat is also introducing a Model Context Protocol server that allows compatible AI assistants to investigate live Linux systems while maintaining access controls. Integration with Performance Co-Pilot, an open-source toolkit for monitoring, recording, analyzing, and controlling infrastructure, enables agents to examine historical performance information alongside current system conditions to identify the causes of operational problems.

A self-managed version of the RHEL command-line assistant, available in developer preview, lets organizations run AI inference locally. The capability is intended for disconnected, air-gapped and regulated environments where sending operational information outside the organization may be prohibited.

The releases also introduce post-quantum cryptography support for applications built using the Go programming language, including integration of the post-quantum Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism encryption algorithm with the language’s Transport Layer Security implementation. Additional enhancements include updated developer toolchains and support for newer processor architectures.

Red Hat separately announced Developer Hub 2.1, an update to its enterprise developer portal that gives AI coding agents governed access to organizational information, approved software components and standardized development workflows. Through MCP integration, agents can discover existing services, follow established development procedures and perform authorized actions using enterprise tooling.

The update also introduces expanded AI asset cataloging, a context-aware assistant and a longer support lifecycle, increasing the release support window from six to 10 months. Developer Hub 2.1 is generally available, as is OpenShift 5, while the new RHEL versions are expected in the coming weeks.

#5538. Cboe Expands Prediction Markets Suite to Small-Caps with Launch of Mini-Russell 2000 Index Binary Options

CHICAGO, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (Cboe: CBOE), a leading global markets operator and pioneer in equity and index derivatives, today announced the launch of mini-Russell 2000 Index (MRUT) binary options (ticker: MRTBW). The binary options based on MRUT, which is 1/10th the size of the Russell 2000 Index, began trading on November 9 and are the latest addition to Cboe's prediction market suite.

MRTBW are yes or no directional trades that pay $100 or $0, depending on whether the MRUT settles at, above or below the specified level. For example, an investor who makes a trade that MRUT will close above 280 will receive $100 at settlement if it closes at 280 or above, while the contract will pay $0 if the index closes below 280. Cboe will list P.M.-settled contracts expiring on the same and next trading day, and MRTBW options offerings are centrally cleared through the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC).

"Small-cap stocks are closely watched by retail investors and can play an important role in a portfolio, and Cboe's new MRUT binary options allow investors to make yes-or-no trades on a leading small-cap index," said JJ Kinahan, Head of Retail Expansion and Alternative Investment Products at Cboe. "The Russell 2000 Index is traditionally more volatile than other broad measures, which is part of why demand for zero-days-to-expiry options tied to the index has grown significantly in recent years. As interest in short-dated exposure grows, Cboe continues to expand its SEC-regulated prediction markets offerings and provide investors with the ability to trade and learn more about market outcomes within the safeguards of the securities markets."

"The Russell 2000 Index is the leading benchmark for the U.S. small-cap equity market, providing investors with a trusted and objective measure of this important market," said Shawn Creighton, Director of Index Derivatives Solutions at FTSE Russell. "Our longstanding partnership with Cboe has been instrumental in expanding access to innovative index-based products, and this latest development builds on that relationship by giving investors more ways to access U.S. small caps and manage risk."

The Russell 2000 Index measures the performance of the small-cap segment of the U.S. equity market. The index includes approximately 2,000 of the smallest companies based on a combination of their market capitalization and current index membership. The Russell 2000 Index is a subset of the Russell 3000 Index, which is designed to represent approximately 98% of the investible U.S. equity market. Cboe has seen record demand in its traditional Russell 2000 Index (RUT) options suite, with average daily volume of 85 thousand contracts through the first three quarters.

With the launch of MRUT binary options, Cboe's prediction markets suite now includes the ability to trade outcomes tied to small-cap and large-cap (S&P 500 Index) equities and will soon include certain SEC-regulated corporate earnings metrics. Cboe's prediction markets offerings are available through select retail brokers and leverage the protections of the U.S. registered securities trading environment.

To learn more about Cboe's offerings, visit Cboe Prediction Markets.

#5535. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5533. NRG Energy is selling $4 billion in natural-gas power plants to LS Power

Free daily briefing on global business news.

NRG said proceeds from the 4.9-gigawatt sale will support additional share repurchases and debt reduction

NRG Energy agreed to sell six power-generation assets totaling 4.9 gigawatts in a $4 billion deal, the company said on Monday. The buyer is LS Power, which will pay $4 billion in cash for the natural gas-fired plants, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The sale is slated to be finalized during 2027’s second quarter, pending regulatory clearances such as Hart-Scott-Rodino and other standard closing requirements, NRG said.

NRG said proceeds will support its 2027 capital allocation plan, additional share repurchases, debt reduction and flexibility to redeploy capital at higher returns. The plan also calls for raising the yearly common dividend, according to The Wall Street Journal.

"Today's announcement is about returning more to our shareholders and supporting future growth investments," NRG CEO Robert Gaudette said, according to The Wall Street Journal.

After the sale is completed, NRG will own and operate 20 GW of generation capacity, the company said. Barclays is serving as lead financial adviser on the transaction. NRG said it will discuss the deal on its earnings conference call.

NRG stock rose 6.4% to $93.96 in premarket trading Monday.

NRG announced the sale with its third-quarter results. The company reported third-quarter net income of $561 million, up from $152 million a year earlier. Adjusted earnings were $4.68 a share, compared with $2.78 a share in the year-earlier quarter.

NRG also issued 2027 guidance of $8.05 to $10.05 in adjusted earnings a share. That range excludes the expected effects of the sale.

#5532. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5531. Empyrean Expands Access to Benefits Administration for Public Sector Organizations Through OMNIA Partners

Competitively awarded cooperative purchasing contract helps government and education organizations simplify procurement and modernize benefits administration.

HOUSTON, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Empyrean, a leading provider of benefits administration technology and services, announced it has been awarded a new cooperative purchasing agreement through OMNIA Partners, making its benefits administration technology and services more accessible to public sector organizations nationwide.

Through the competitively solicited contract, eligible government agencies, educational institutions, and other public sector organizations can more easily access Empyrean's configurable benefits administration platform and expert services, helping reduce procurement complexity and accelerate benefits modernization.

Public sector benefits leaders face distinct challenges, from managing diverse employee populations and intricate eligibility requirements to navigating evolving regulations and increasing pressure on administrative resources. Empyrean helps public sector organizations manage that complexity through reliable benefits administration, intelligent technology, and dedicated experts who understand each organization's unique requirements. Together, they help keep benefits accurate, administration manageable, and employees supported at every stage of their benefits journey.

"Public sector benefits teams are responsible for getting some of the most important details in their employees' lives right, often while navigating complex requirements and limited resources," said Jim Priebe, Chief Strategy Officer at Empyrean. "Through OMNIA Partners, we're making it easier for these organizations to access the technology and hands-on expertise they need to administer benefits confidently, and deliver a better experience for the people they serve."

Benefits Administration Built for Public Sector Needs

Empyrean's configurable benefits administration platform, paired with experienced implementation and service teams, supports the unique needs of public sector organizations, including diverse workforces, union and non-union populations, complex eligibility structures, and organization-specific business rules.

Together, Empyrean's technology and services help organizations:

Empyrean brings over two decades of benefits administration experience to organizations with sophisticated benefits requirements. That expertise, combined with a commitment to accountable service and lasting client partnerships, is reflected in its 98% client retention rate.

Expanding Access Through Cooperative Purchasing

OMNIA Partners is a leading public sector cooperative purchasing organization that connects agencies with competitively solicited contracts and trusted suppliers. Through this agreement, eligible organizations can access Empyrean's solutions using an established cooperative purchasing vehicle, helping streamline the purchasing process while supporting their procurement objectives.

"Benefits administration touches every employee, and the teams responsible for it deserve partners who make their work easier, not harder," said Doug Looney, Senior Vice President for Partner Development at OMNIA Partners. "Empyrean brings deep expertise and technology built for the realities of public sector organizations. Through this competitively solicited contract, our members get a trusted way to put that support to work without starting a new bid process, so they can spend less time on paperwork and more time serving their people. We're proud to welcome Empyrean to the OMNIA Partners supplier community."

The contract, Solutions for Public Sector Business Processes, Operations, and Finance, was awarded through Region 14 Education Service Center.

#5530. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

#5528. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

#5526. Opinion: San Francisco is delivering, while Seattle is still deliberating

by Joe Nguyễn on Nov 3, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 3, 2026 at 9:47 am

Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email [email protected].

How can a region care so much, spend billions in tax dollars and yet leave people losing faith in its future?

In Seattle, that question has become painfully familiar. People see suffering and disorder on their streets with little reason to believe help is coming. Business owners wonder whether the city values their presence or understands what it takes to keep their doors open. Even people who love this place are beginning to speak about its problems as permanent.

That growing resignation took us to San Francisco. We wanted to understand how a city so many had written off was giving people reasons to believe in its future again.

I expected to come home impressed with San Francisco. Instead, I came home with a deeper appreciation for Seattle. And an anger I am still trying to reconcile.

Seeing San Francisco make progress reminded me that Seattle has the talent and resources to do the same, perhaps even better. That is what made me frustrated. We should not have to accept people suffering on our streets and businesses struggling to stay open as conditions beyond our ability to change.

Not long ago, San Francisco had become a warning about what happens when a prosperous city loses its way. Less than two years into Mayor Daniel Lurie’s administration, that story has begun to change. Reported crime fell 22 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. According to Kidder Mathews, office vacancy declined to 26 percent in the third quarter from 31 percent in the prior year.

San Francisco still has profound problems, and the suffering we saw on its streets cannot be erased by encouraging statistics. But the people we met shared a confidence that their work could change the city’s direction. They understood what they were working toward and could explain what would happen next. Their optimism comes from seeing progress and believing they can build on it.

And I kept wondering why that felt so refreshing.

Seattle has extraordinary talent and resources, with public servants who care deeply and service providers doing demanding work under difficult conditions. Our business community helps shape the world. With that much ability and commitment here, we should feel confident that we can make our own neighborhoods safer and more welcoming.

Yet we often seem more resigned to our limitations than confident in our possibilities.

I recognize that habit because I have worked inside it. As a legislator and state agency director, I saw good intentions fall short when leaders avoided hard decisions and failed to hold people accountable for results. Even small obstacles became accepted excuses when no one took responsibility for overcoming them.

Throughout the trip, I kept looking for a more complicated explanation for the difference between San Francisco and Seattle. Eventually, the answer became impossible to miss.

Leaders expected the institutions they led to deliver results and took responsibility for making that happen. The unsettling part was how unfamiliar something so basic had come to feel.

San Francisco offered examples of what happens when leaders refuse to accept failure.

“Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.”

One example was Mayor Lurie’s response to open-air drug markets. The previous administration had already brought police, public health officials and other agencies together, but people we met described meetings that produced more updates than action. Lurie took that existing structure and gave it a clear purpose. Participants were expected to make decisions and take responsibility for carrying them out, then return with evidence of what had changed on the streets.

This approach helped illuminate a problem that is also familiar to Seattle. Officers encountering someone dangerously intoxicated often have no appropriate place to take them. Leaving the person on the street puts them and others at risk, while taking them to jail does little to address their need for care and would remove scarce law enforcement officials from patrol for hours.

San Francisco opened the RESET Center to fill this gap. Eligible individuals are able to receive brief medical supervision and stabilization, followed by connections to services. The center opened within ten months of the decision to proceed. It is a limited response to a larger crisis, but it gives people an option they lacked.

Across our conversations, leadership meant staying with a problem until the next step became possible. That requires something more uncomfortable than calling for accountability. It requires accepting that evidence may challenge an approach we have previously defended.

If we believe Seattle is a progressive city, we should ask whether our policies deliver the progress we promise. That means questioning our assumptions and changing programs when results fall short. Reconsidering an approach can feel like abandoning our values, but those values should compel us to change when people are still in need of help.

The business community must reconsider its own habits too. We often avoid politics even as public decisions shape our future. In San Francisco, business leaders helped set the agenda and backed leaders willing to act. If we want better outcomes here, we must help shape the decisions that produce them.

Government, in turn, must make clear that businesses belong here. A shop owner asking for a safe doorway and a person in crisis outside that door both deserve a response. A capable city should be able to care for both.

People form their judgment of a city through these encounters. They notice whether someone answers. They notice whether anything changes.

Over time, those experiences become confidence or despair.

San Francisco reminded me that resignation can lift. People can begin expecting more when they see reasons to believe their efforts matter.

Seattle has so much worth believing in. What we need is leadership willing to turn that promise into something people can feel.

Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.

What might we accomplish if we recovered it?

#5525. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nvidia's board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised as Huang's ties to the suspected spy have roiled the company

Samuel Boivin / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Nvidia $NVDA's board of directors launched an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang on Sunday, and the company's stock fell in premarket trading on Monday.

Nvidia stock was down about 5% to 6% in premarket trading. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the inquiry, the company said.

The board said the investigation follows recent reporting that Huang had been singled out by a foreign intelligence effort. It said it has seen nothing to suggest that national security or Nvidia's confidential information was put at risk, and that the inquiry will examine all available information. The board said it stands behind Huang and his leadership team, and that Huang backs the review and has pledged to cooperate.

Huang acknowledged an affair in a message to employees. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang wrote.

Reports identify the woman as Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed International whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China. Alice Huang is no relation to the Nvidia CEO. A memo passed around Washington policy circles earlier in 2026 alleged that China's Ministry of State Security had enlisted her to gather intelligence on Nvidia's CEO.

China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, according to CNBC.

President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Huang is "an honorable guy" who has done "an amazing job for our country." Trump has said Huang should stay on as CEO.

Three House Republican committee chairs asked Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18, in a letter sent last week. Sen. Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat, vowed to look into the issu. Megaspeed has said it is a “compliant and legitimate company.” An Nvidia spokesperson said Huang is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.

Nvidia stock has slid roughly 22% since hitting its peak in October. The company is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.

#5519. Alphabet might sell its first Hong Kong and Singapore dollar bonds as soon as this month

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Alphabet is weighing raising the equivalent of $1 billion to $1.5 billion in Hong Kong dollars and about $1.5 billion in Singapore dollars

Alphabet $GOOGL, the parent of Google, has held talks about selling its first bonds denominated in Hong Kong and Singapore dollars, according to Bloomberg.

Alphabet has approached banks and investors to discuss a possible debt offering, which could come as soon as this month, according to Bloomberg. Alphabet is aiming for the Hong Kong dollar portion to be worth between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, while the Singapore dollar portion would be roughly $1.5 billion, with proceeds earmarked for general corporate purposes.

Discussions remain active, and the specifics of the offering may yet shift, according to Bloomberg. Alphabet declined to comment on market speculation.

A deal would gauge how much demand Asian investors have for such debt in the wake of a worldwide market rout driven by AI worries, according to Bloomberg. Investors are uneasy that AI-related projects could face tougher oversight now that Democrats have picked up ground in the midterm elections in the U.S. Credit spreads on the debt of certain tech issuers have widened, compounding a repricing across worldwide bond markets, where yields have climbed as AI-boom borrowing piled up.

Alphabet, Microsoft $MSFT, Amazon $AMZN and Meta $META Platforms have been issuing debt at an unprecedented rate while also earmarking sums in the tens of billions for AI capabilities, according to Bloomberg. Hyperscalers have been branching out into debt markets that were previously untouched by them in their hunt for additional funding.

Alphabet's first Australian dollar bond sale came in August, according to Bloomberg. Before that offering, the company set out to raise about A$5 billion ($3.6 billion) across four tranches, with the longest running 20 years. Alphabet has also issued notes this year in Swiss francs, British pounds, Canadian dollars and Japanese yen, according to Bloomberg.

Last week, Alphabet brought in €6 billion ($6.7 billion) by selling euro bonds in several tranches, marking its second offering denominated in euros so far this year, according to Bloomberg. The company had to accept noticeably steeper borrowing costs than it did on its debut euro deal in May, as worries mounted about how quickly AI spending is rising.

Meta Platforms also moved to market U.S. dollar bonds last week under a plan to borrow at least $20 billion across the U.S. and Europe.
