#5500. From the 1845 law to midnight votes, 15 facts about how Election Day works

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The reason Americans vote on a Tuesday goes back to an 1845 law and a farm calendar, and 15 slides trace the history through ballots, amendments and traditions

The U.S. picks its presidents on a schedule designed for a very different country. When Congress settled on a single national voting day in 1845, most Americans lived in rural areas and worked in agriculture. Many had to reach a county seat to cast a ballot, and that trip could take a day or more. The calendar lawmakers chose reflected long trips, harvests and Sunday worship — not office jobs, commutes or mail-in ballots.

That 1845 law fixed the date for choosing presidential electors as the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. It said nothing about why. The usual reasons come from historical accounts, not from the statute's text. They include a harvest finished by November, roads still passable before winter and a Sunday kept free of travel. Other stories, such as Wednesday being market day, get repeated so often that they sound settled. They are commonly cited explanations, not documented ones.

Knowing why Americans vote on a Tuesday also explains how the rest of the system grew around that date. Before 1845, states set their own dates within a window Congress allowed, and voting stretched across weeks. In 1872, Congress extended the same November date to House elections. Senate races joined after the 17th Amendment gave voters, not state legislatures, the power to elect senators. The date stayed put while the rules about who could vote, and how, changed around it.

The secret ballot replaced the often public practice of voting by voice or with party-printed tickets. Constitutional amendments protected women's right to vote, banned poll taxes in federal elections and set the voting age at 18. Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in 1965. Each shift happened on top of a calendar first drawn for a farming economy.

The first slides cover the calendar itself: the law, the month, the weekday and the specific phrasing that keeps Election Day from ever landing on Nov. 1. The next group traces how elections for Congress joined the same date and how access to the ballot widened. The last group looks at the traditions and rules that surround the day now. Those include a New Hampshire town's midnight vote and the fact that Election Day is not a federal holiday. They also compare how other democracies schedule elections and trace the weeks between the vote and the inauguration.

Americans vote on a Tuesday because of a federal law Congress passed in 1845. It set one national day for choosing presidential electors: the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. That rule still fixes the date of presidential elections.

The law covered presidential elections only. It did not set the timing of congressional races, which stayed under state control for decades afterward. Voters were also not choosing a president directly. They were choosing the electors who would cast the formal votes for president on behalf of each state.

Congress had clear authority to act. Article II of the Constitution lets Congress determine the time of choosing electors and the day on which they give their votes. It also requires that the electors' voting day be the same throughout the nation. The 1845 statute used that power to fix a single Election Day for the whole country.

President John Tyler signed the measure in January 1845. The 1844 race had already been decided under the older arrangement. The new rule first applied four years later. The 1848 contest was the first presidential election held under the single-day system. Zachary Taylor, the Whig candidate, won it.

The law also included a fallback provision. It allowed a state that failed to make a choice on Election Day to appoint its electors on a later day. The state legislature could direct how that later appointment happened. That clause stayed on the books for more than 170 years. Congress narrowed it in the Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022. The newer law permits a state to extend its voting period only for extraordinary and catastrophic events.

The 1845 law set the timing of the choice, not its method. Each state legislature still decided how its electors would be appointed. South Carolina's legislature kept picking the state's electors itself, rather than holding a popular vote, until after the Civil War. The Election Day rule now sits in Title 3 of the U.S. Code, the part of federal law that governs presidential elections.

Election Day was built around the working life of the American farmer. According to the standard historical account, when Congress set a national voting date in 1845, the calendar had to suit a country where most voters lived and worked on farms.

Distance was the central problem. For many rural voters, casting a ballot meant traveling to the county seat. That trip could take a day or more.

Travel moved at the pace of a horse. In the 1840s, a voter generally made the journey on horseback, by wagon or on foot. Most roads were unpaved. Rain could turn those dirt roads to mud and lengthen the trip. Railroads were still new and covered only a small part of the country. Few farm families could count on a train to reach the polls.

A trip of that length turned voting into an errand measured in days, not hours. A voter had to leave home, reach the polling place, cast a ballot and then make the return journey.

For a farm family, each of those days carried a cost. Time on the road was time away from crops and livestock. In the standard account, a workable date had to leave room for the journey in both directions, not only for the moment at the ballot box.

That logic belonged to the electorate of the 1840s. The U.S. later became a mostly urban country. The 1920 census was the first to count more Americans living in urban areas than in rural ones. For that count, the Census Bureau treated places with 2,500 or more residents as urban. That crossover arrived 75 years after the 1845 law.

The federal voting date did not move with that shift. Election Day still falls on the schedule Congress fixed in 1845, when reaching the polls could mean a day or more on the road.

Election Day landed on Tuesday largely by elimination. Sunday was reserved for worship, and a Monday vote would have forced many voters to travel on Sunday.

The Sunday problem was the simplest to see. In the mid-1800s, Sunday was a day of worship for much of the country. Holding an election on it would have put civic duty in direct competition with church. The national date Congress set in 1845 kept voting off the Sabbath.

Monday created a second-order problem. Rural voters who lived far from the polls needed travel time before they could cast a ballot. A Monday election would have meant leaving home on Sunday. That ran into the same objection that ruled out Sunday voting itself. Tuesday gave those voters a full day to make the trip after worship.

Wednesday is where the history gets less certain. A frequently repeated account holds that Wednesday was market day in many places, when farmers brought goods to town to sell. Under that account, a Wednesday election would have cut into a working day that rural families depended on.

That market-day explanation is a commonly cited reason, not documented intent. The 1845 statute fixes the date without recording a rationale for any weekday. The reasons attached to it today are reconstructions built from the conditions of the period. They are not language written into the law.

Taken together, the three constraints point toward a narrow window. A voter could attend worship on Sunday, travel on Monday and cast a ballot on Tuesday. Under the market-day account, that voter could also be back for Wednesday's trading. The commonly repeated explanation does not address Thursday, Friday or Saturday, and the law itself is silent on them too.

The result has outlasted the farm economy that shaped it. The same Tuesday rule still governs federal elections, even though few Americans now farm or plan their week around a town market.

Election Day falls in November because the month offered a workable window in a farming country. The standard historical explanation holds that the harvest was largely finished by then, while winter had not yet closed the roads.

That explanation comes from historical accounts, not from the law. The 1845 statute that created a single national date for choosing presidential electors names the month without explaining it.

The farm side of the reasoning follows the agricultural year. Spring meant planting. Summer and early autumn meant tending and gathering crops. A vote during those months would have pulled people away from the fields at the busiest time. Much of that work was done by November.

The weather side concerns travel. Many voters went to the polls by horse, by wagon or on foot over unpaved roads. Snow, ice and mud could make those routes hard or impossible to use later in the year. An early November vote came before the worst of winter across much of the country.

Those conditions were not the same everywhere. Winter arrived far earlier in New England than along the Gulf Coast. The 1845 law still set one national date for every state.

The November timing also fit the federal schedule already in place. A 1792 law had let states choose electors during a window that closed before the electors met in December. The 1845 date fell inside that window, so the electors' December meeting did not have to move.

The first presidential election held on the uniform date took place on Nov. 7, 1848. Federal law still sets the presidential vote in November, in Title 3 of the U.S. Code. That vote comes every fourth year, in years divisible by four, such as 2024 and 2028. The date has outlasted the farm economy that is said to have shaped it.

The phrase "the Tuesday after the first Monday in November" fixes federal Election Day to a date between Nov. 2 and Nov. 8. That wording means the vote can never land on Nov. 1, even in years when the month begins on a Tuesday.

The rule works in two steps. Find the first Monday of November, then move forward one day. A simpler instruction, such as "the first Tuesday in November," would put the election on Nov. 1 whenever the month opens on a Tuesday. The extra step removes that possibility.

The 2016 presidential election shows the formula at work. Nov. 1, 2016, fell on a Tuesday, so the first Monday of that month was Nov. 7. Voters went to the polls the next day, Nov. 8. That is the latest date the formula allows.

The other end of the range appears when November starts on a Monday. In 2004, Nov. 1 was a Monday, which made Nov. 2 Election Day. The 2020 election, held on Nov. 3, landed near the start of the window.

The 1845 law that created the formula does not say why lawmakers wrote it this way. Two reasons for keeping the vote off Nov. 1 are commonly cited. Both are later explanations, not reasons recorded in the statute.

The first involves All Saints' Day. The Christian feast falls on Nov. 1. For Roman Catholics, it is a holy day of obligation, when attendance at Mass is expected. The explanation holds that lawmakers wanted to avoid scheduling a national vote on a major religious observance.

The second involves commerce. Merchants are often said to have used the first of the month to close out the previous month's accounts. Under this account, a Nov. 1 vote would have collided with a day many business owners set aside for bookkeeping.

The result is a window of seven possible dates. The formula depends only on the calendar, so any future Election Day can be worked out years ahead. The 2028 presidential election, for example, falls on Nov. 7.

Before 1845, there was no single Election Day for president. Each state picked its own date for choosing presidential electors, as long as it fell inside a window Congress set in 1792.

That 1792 federal law gave states a 34-day window. Electors could be appointed at any point during the 34 days before the first Wednesday in December, the day the electors then met to vote. A state could hold its contest early in that span or late in it.

The Constitution made this arrangement possible. Article II gives Congress the power to set the time for choosing electors and the day on which electors cast their votes. It requires that the electors' voting day be the same throughout the U.S. It sets no such uniformity rule for choosing the electors themselves. Until 1845, Congress left that timing to the states within the federal window.

Article II also leaves the method of appointing electors to each state legislature. In the early decades, many legislatures chose electors themselves instead of holding a popular vote. By the 1830s, South Carolina was the only state still doing so. Its legislature kept picking the state's electors through the 1860 election. Where a popular vote did happen, the state set its own date for it.

The practical result was a presidential election spread across weeks. Voters in one state could go to the polls well before voters in another. The national contest unfolded in pieces, with each state on its own schedule.

That staggered calendar created a timing problem. Results from states that voted early could become known before other states had voted at all. Voters in later states could cast ballots after some of those outcomes were already known.

That problem is a commonly cited reason for a single national day. Congress settled the question in 1845. It replaced the open window with one fixed date for choosing presidential electors in every state.

Congress put elections for the U.S. House of Representatives on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November through a law passed in 1872. That measure gave House races the same national date already used for choosing presidential electors.

The 1872 law arrived 27 years after the 1845 statute that first created a single national Election Day. The earlier law covered presidential elections only. It set no date for congressional contests.

Before 1872, each state picked its own date for House elections. Some states held those races on the same day as presidential voting. Others held them on different days. The country had no single date for choosing its representatives.

The Constitution's Elections Clause gave Congress the authority to make the change. The clause leaves the times, places and manner of congressional elections to state legislatures. It also lets Congress make or alter those rules. The 1872 law used that federal power to set one date for House races across the country.

After 1872, House elections shared the November date with presidential voting. The Constitution puts every House seat up for election every two years. As a result, the law placed a federal contest on the November ballot in years without a presidential race, too.

U.S. Senate seats were not part of this change. State legislatures still chose senators at the time, so there was no popular Senate vote to schedule.

Voters have elected U.S. senators directly only since 1913, when the 17th Amendment was ratified. Before that, state legislatures chose senators. The change moved Senate races onto the same national November date that voters already used for other federal offices.

The original Constitution set up the Senate differently from the House. Article I, Section 3 gave each state two senators. It also said they would be chosen by the state's legislature for six-year terms. House members, by contrast, were elected by the people from the start. The framers designed the two chambers to answer to different constituencies.

Under that system, a voter's influence over the Senate was indirect. Citizens elected state lawmakers, and those lawmakers then picked the senators. A Senate seat could hinge on which party controlled a state legislature rather than on a statewide vote.

The 17th Amendment rewrote that arrangement. Its text provides that the Senate is made up of two senators from each state, elected by the people of that state, for six years. It also requires voters in Senate elections to meet the same qualifications as voters for the most numerous branch of their state legislature. That wording tied eligibility for Senate voting to rules each state already used.

The amendment also addressed vacancies. It directs a state's governor to call an election to fill an open seat. A state legislature may empower the governor to make a temporary appointment until voters fill the seat.

Once senators were chosen by popular vote, their races joined the federal ballot on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. Presidential, House and Senate contests now share that date.

The six-year term did not change. Senate terms are staggered. About one-third of the seats come up in each two-year election cycle. As a result, each regular November general election includes Senate races in only some states. Every House seat, by contrast, is on the ballot each time.

The secret ballot let Americans mark a government-printed ballot in private, replacing a system in which many votes were cast in public. Massachusetts adopted the approach statewide in 1888, and other states followed over the next several years.

Before that shift, casting a vote was often a visible act. In some places, voters announced their choices aloud at the polling place. Elsewhere, they handed in tickets printed and distributed by political parties rather than by election officials.

A party ticket usually listed only that party's candidates. A voter could pick one up from a party worker, carry it to the polls and drop it in the ballot box. The paper itself could show anyone watching which side a voter supported.

That visibility had consequences. An employer, a landlord or a party operative standing near the polls could see how a person voted. Someone paying for votes could confirm that the purchase had been delivered. Voters who depended on others for work or housing had reason to think twice before breaking with them in public.

The reform became known as the Australian ballot. It took that name because the colony of Victoria, in Australia, introduced it in 1856, decades before it reached the U.S. Under the system, election officials, not parties, printed the ballots. Every qualifying candidate appeared on the same sheet. Voters marked their choices out of view of others.

Private marking meant a vote buyer could no longer check what a voter had done. A single official ballot listing all candidates made it easier to choose people from different parties in the same election. Government printing also meant the state now had to decide whose names appeared on the ballot. That pushed lawmakers to write rules for how candidates qualified.

The ballot most Americans fill out on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November descends from this late-19th-century design. The private voting booth, the uniform official ballot and the expectation that no one else sees a voter's choices all trace back to it.

The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, bars the federal government and the states from denying the vote on account of sex. The presidential election of Nov. 2, 1920 was the first in which women across the country could vote with that right protected by the Constitution.

The amendment's core text is a single sentence. It says the right of citizens of the U.S. to vote "shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex." A second section gives Congress the power to enforce that guarantee through legislation.

The proposal took more than four decades to clear Congress. Sen. Aaron Sargent of California introduced the language in 1878. It became known as the Susan B. Anthony Amendment. The House approved it on May 21, 1919. The Senate followed on June 4, 1919, sending it to the states.

Ratification required approval from three-fourths of the 48 states then in the union. Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify on Aug. 18, 1920. That vote supplied the final approval needed. Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certified the amendment on Aug. 26, 1920.

The November vote that followed kept the schedule Congress had set in 1845. Nov. 2, 1920 was the Tuesday after the first Monday of the month. Republican Warren G. Harding defeated Democrat James M. Cox in that race.

The push for a national guarantee began long before 1920. The Seneca Falls Convention in New York issued a call for women's voting rights in 1848. Wyoming's territorial legislature granted women the vote in 1869. Several Western states extended full voting rights to women before the amendment took effect. The 19th Amendment replaced that state-by-state patchwork with a constitutional standard.

The amendment did not put a ballot in every woman's hand in practice. Many Black women in Southern states stayed blocked by the same discriminatory registration rules used against Black men. Many Native American women could not vote because the U.S. did not yet recognize them as citizens. Congress passed the Indian Citizenship Act in 1924. Some states still restricted Native voting for years afterward.

Three changes between 1964 and 1971 widened who could cast a ballot on Election Day. The 24th Amendment, ratified in 1964, banned poll taxes in federal elections. The Voting Rights Act became law in 1965. The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971, set the voting age at 18.

A poll tax was a fee charged as a condition of voting. By the 1960s it survived mainly in Southern states. There it had long served to keep Black voters and poor white voters away from the polls. The 24th Amendment covered only federal races — presidential, Senate and House contests. Its text left state and local elections untouched.

That gap closed two years later. In Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections, decided in 1966, the Supreme Court ruled that poll taxes in state elections violated the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment. The amendment and the ruling, taken together, ended the practice.

The Voting Rights Act reached further than the poll tax ban. President Lyndon B. Johnson signed it on Aug. 6, 1965. That came months after state troopers attacked civil rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama. The law targeted tools such as literacy tests, which local officials had used to turn away Black applicants. It also allowed federal examiners to register voters in some places.

One of its central provisions, known as preclearance, required jurisdictions covered by the law to get federal approval before changing their voting rules. In Shelby County v. Holder, decided in 2013, the Supreme Court struck down the formula that determined which jurisdictions were covered. Without a valid formula, the preclearance requirement no longer applies to the jurisdictions it once covered. Other parts of the act remain in force.

The 26th Amendment lowered the minimum voting age to 18 in federal, state and local elections. Before it, most states set the minimum at 21. The push gained force during the Vietnam War. Men could be drafted at 18, but in most states they could not vote. Supporters rallied around the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote."

Congress had first tried to lower the age by statute. In Oregon v. Mitchell, decided in 1970, the Supreme Court ruled that Congress could set an 18-year-old voting age for federal elections but not for state ones. That split would have forced many states to run separate voting systems for different races. A constitutional amendment resolved the problem, and the states ratified it in 1971.

Dixville Notch, a small town in New Hampshire, casts its Election Day ballots at midnight, in the first minutes of the voting day. The town has held this midnight vote since 1960.

Federal Election Day falls on a Tuesday. In Dixville Notch, voting begins as soon as Monday night turns into Tuesday morning. Most polling places in the U.S. open hours later, in the morning. That timing puts the town's ballots in before most of the country has started voting.

The tradition started in a presidential election year. The town has repeated the midnight vote in the decades since. Its ballots are now among the first cast on Election Day in the U.S.

The early start changes only when residents vote, not the rules they vote under. Dixville Notch uses the same national date as every other community. Its ballots count toward New Hampshire's results the same way any other town's do.

Election Day is a regular working day in the U.S. Federal law fixes the date for federal elections, but no federal law makes that Tuesday a federal holiday.

That leaves time off to the states. Some states have their own provisions that give workers time off to vote. Others treat Election Day as a state holiday. The rules vary, so what a voter can expect depends on where they live and work.

The date and the holiday question sit in different parts of federal law. The 1845 law and the statutes that followed it set when federal elections take place. Federal holidays are listed separately, in Title 5, Section 6103, of the U.S. Code, and Election Day is not among them.

The list sets paid days off for federal employees. Federal law does not require private employers to close on any of those days. Federal offices stay open on Election Day, and it runs like any other Tuesday on the federal calendar.

One federal holiday sits close by. Veterans Day falls on Nov. 11. Federal Election Day can land no later than Nov. 8, so the two never coincide. Veterans Day arrives three to nine days after the vote.

For voters, working-day status shapes the time they have. People with fixed shifts who vote in person that day must go before work, after work or during a break, unless they get time off. Many states also offer early in-person voting or mail ballots, which let people vote without a Tuesday trip to the polls. Polling hours, which states set, decide how much room the day itself leaves.

The result is a split system. The date is national and fixed by federal law. Any time away from work to use it comes from state law, an employer's own policy or a voter's own schedule.

Germany holds its federal elections on Sundays, while U.K. general elections have traditionally fallen on Thursdays. Many other countries also schedule national votes on weekends. The American Tuesday is one answer among several to the question of when a country should vote.

Germany's Sunday schedule moves the federal vote outside the Monday-to-Friday workweek. A voter on a standard weekday schedule does not have to arrange time off, leave early or line up before a shift to take part.

The U.K. custom sits closer to the American model. Thursday, like Tuesday, falls in the middle of the working week. Voters with weekday jobs in either country have to fit a trip to the polling place around their hours on the job.

Weekend voting in other countries follows the same reasoning as Germany's Sunday elections. For people who work Monday through Friday, a Saturday or Sunday vote falls on a day off. The trade-off runs the other way for people whose jobs include weekend shifts. They face the same scheduling problem a weekday voter faces in the U.S. or U.K.

Set side by side, these approaches show that the day of the week is a choice each country makes, not a fixed feature of national elections. Germany and many other countries put the vote on a weekend. The U.K. and the U.S. keep it on a weekday.

Election Day does not install a president. Voters choose electors in November, those electors cast the formal votes in December, and the new term begins at noon on Jan. 20 under the 20th Amendment, ratified in 1933.

The electors meet in their own states rather than in one national gathering. The Constitution requires that arrangement. Under the 12th Amendment, each state's electors cast separate ballots for president and vice president. The results are sealed and sent to Washington, D.C.

Electors are chosen through the popular vote in each state. Their December ballots are the formal step between November's results and the official count in Congress.

Congress then counts the electoral votes in a joint session in January. The sitting vice president, acting as president of the Senate, opens the certificates. A candidate needs a majority of the 538 electoral votes, which is 270, to win outright. If no one reaches that mark, the House of Representatives chooses the president. In that case, each state delegation casts one vote.

For most of the country's history, the wait was far longer. Presidents took office on March 4, a date tied to the start of the federal government under the Constitution in 1789. That left about four months between the November vote and the transfer of power.

The long gap had real consequences. After Abraham Lincoln won in November 1860, seven Southern states seceded before he took office in March 1861. James Buchanan remained president through that winter.

The 20th Amendment cut the presidential wait by roughly six weeks. It also moved the start of new congressional terms to Jan. 3. As a result, a newly elected Congress is seated before it counts the electoral votes. The measure is often called the lame duck amendment. It shortened the period that outgoing officials, known as lame ducks, serve after an election.

Franklin D. Roosevelt was the last president first inaugurated on March 4, in 1933. His second inauguration, in 1937, was the first held on Jan. 20.

#5499. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5498. After Elizabeth Holmes Ate His Product, Everything Changed for His Business: ‘This Publicity, It’s in the Millions of Dollars’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Ricky Hirsch, founder of Think Jerky, was “overwhelmed” when his brand appeared on screen.

On October 16, Ricky Hirsch’s meat snack startup Think Jerky experienced an unscripted marketing moment so crazy it’s “not even once in a lifetime,” the founder and CEO tells Entrepreneur.

Hirsch launched Think Jerky in 2015, building on his finance background and creative inclinations to start a “cool” jerky brand with a minimalist design and unique, chef-crafted flavors.

The brand’s sriracha honey flavor, created by Michelin-starred and two-time James Beard Award-winning chef Gale Gand, landed in the spotlight last month.

Hirsch was watching poker on television at his home in Austin, Texas, when he received a text from one of his employees.

She was in New York and had just attended a screening of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 meta-documentary featuring Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the lead-up to her federal prison sentence.

Holmes was convicted of one count of conspiracy alongside three wire fraud charges stemming from more than $140 million in investor losses in 2022.

“ I was familiar with Elizabeth Holmes,” Hirsch says. “I’m in the business world, so that always intrigued me. And I saw the Hulu series. I was not familiar with Nathan Fielder at all.”

Hirsch’s employee was “freaking out” over Think Jerky’s cameo, the founder recalls.

In You Can See Everything, Holmes requests turkey jerky from the prison vending machine. The scene is reenacted with Amanda Seyfried, who plays Holmes in Hulu’s The Dropout. At one point, the camera pans to the vending machine — “it’s like product placement, the best, most beautiful shot,” Hirsch says.

The film ends with Holmes and her husband Billy Evans eating Think Jerky.

Hirsch decided to see the film for himself the next day, but he still had no idea how much the on-screen moment would change his business. “I brought some jerky with me,” Hirsch says. “And when it came on screen, I was overwhelmed. I was like, This is wild.”

The founder walked out of the theater in Austin with about 30 bags of jerky in tow. He started handing them out to people — and they “were freaking out.” It was a sign of things to come.

Within two weeks, Think Jerky’s honey sriracha sales were up 345% on the company’s website and 92% on Amazon. Someone posted on X that the Texas supermarket chain H-E-B had sold out of “the Elizabeth Holmes jerky.”

Reddit forums dissected what Think Jerky might represent as a narrative symbol. (“They think it symbolizes manipulation or control. There’s all these theories”). Fans dressed up as the Think Jerky bag for Halloween (“You have to make that costume”). YouTube videos discussed it. Restaurants reached out for collaborations. People hawked fake merchandise.

“If somebody wanted to pay for this publicity, it’s in the millions of dollars,” Hirsch says.

Hirsch chalks up some of the virality to how the brand’s name — “Think” Jerky — plays right into the “wild,” layered film and becomes its own sort of small character.

Now, the founder is determined to add as much fuel to the marketing fire as possible.

But that’s a tall order for a fully bootstrapped company with four employees. “People are stepping up, our significant others are stepping up and all that, but we are not a big business,” Hirsch says. “We do not have a big team. We never raised money, which is very unique in my industry.”

Hirsch acknowledges that people might not remember Think Jerky’s logo or company name in five years, but they might remember the shot of that bag. So he’s doing his best to make it a meme and keep the conversation going.

The team is going to San Diego for the Food & Wine festival. Gale Gand will make an egg dish (another humorous nod to the film) and top it with the jerky. The team is also planning lookalike contests, where they’ll hand out jerky and display a cutout of Holmes.

Sales remain strong, and Hirsch anticipates selling out. Think Jerky has about 60 days’ worth of finished inventory in reserve to meet the demand.

Currently, the brand is revamping its website, which will be complete in about a month, for a “soft rebrand” that fully captures the product’s chef-crafted approach. Think Jerky is also launching new products, including a Thanksgiving turkey stick made with four-time James Beard Award-winner Andrew Zimmern.

Looking ahead, Hirsch would be very interested in raising money for Think Jerky with the right partner. “ If Daniel Lubetzky wants to talk to me, I would love to talk to Daniel Lubetzky,” the founder says.

Hirsch is excited to continue leaning into Think Jerky’s surprise breakout and explosive growth.

“ I thought it was going fade maybe, after the third weekend, but it’s growing,” Hirsch says. “People are reaching out, people want to collaborate. I want to introduce my creative marketing and hopefully bring our company to a new level.”

On October 16, Ricky Hirsch’s meat snack startup Think Jerky experienced an unscripted marketing moment so crazy it’s “not even once in a lifetime,” the founder and CEO tells Entrepreneur.

Hirsch launched Think Jerky in 2015, building on his finance background and creative inclinations to start a “cool” jerky brand with a minimalist design and unique, chef-crafted flavors.

The brand’s sriracha honey flavor, created by Michelin-starred and two-time James Beard Award-winning chef Gale Gand, landed in the spotlight last month.

#5497. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5496. This Violinist Beat 350,000 Applicants to Become Snoop Dogg’s $10,000-a-Month Ice Cream Taster — Here’s How She Struck a Chord

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Concert violinist Annabelle Traves explains how she scored a $10,000-a-month gig tasting ice cream for Snoop Dogg’s company

How did Annabelle Traves land the sweetest job on the planet? Let’s just say she pulled some strings.

The concert violinist, who has soloed at Carnegie Hall and the Sydney Opera House, was just named Dr. Bombay’s first International Ice Cream Taster. In August, Snoop Dogg’s ice cream brand put out a call for the job, which pays $10,000 a month. More than 350,000 people from 130+ countries applied through HR and payroll platform Deel, which ran the search.

Traves, an Australian based in Dubai, starts a three-month contract helping Dr. Bombay expand into new markets, dream up new flavors and create a Deel-themed ice cream. Entrepreneur caught up with Traves to talk about her latest gig.

What did you submit to beat out all those other applicants?I decided to play to my strengths. Many of the other applicants owned dairy farms or had spent years researching dairy. I love ice cream, but I wouldn’t call myself a dairy expert, so I leaned on what I knew best. In my application video, I plucked a little of one of Snoop’s famous melodies on my violin. When I made the top 15, I doubled down with my own cover of “Young, Wild & Free.” I think that musical connection is part of what caught Snoop’s attention.

You’re already a very successful violinist. Why go after a gig like this?The timing was perfect. I had just come off a world tour with André Rieu, and for the first time in years I didn’t have a schedule that I had to coordinate a year in advance. Then there was the ice cream, and who doesn’t love ice cream? And of course, Snoop himself. I love all genres of music and have always loved his, so the chance to bond with him as a fellow musician was hugely appealing.

What do you look for when you’re tasting a new flavor?In one word, novelty. I want a flavor I’ve never tried before. Vanilla has been done a billion times. Dr. Maya, who develops the flavors at Dr. Bombay, introduced me to the idea that ice cream flavors develop over time. A couple of seconds in, a different flavor comes through. People talk about that with wine, but I’d never experienced such sophisticated flavors in ice cream until I tried Dr. Bombay. The nostalgia of the brand also stands out. Flavors like Sherbet take you right back as a 90s kid, and Peanut Butter Jelly Time does the same. I’d love to find flavors based on popular candies or afternoon snacks from those days.

#5495. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5494. How I Built a Fully Remote Global Team Without Spending a Dollar on Job Ads or Recruiters

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Solopreneurs that provide digital services have a world of talent at their disposal. Here is how to leverage it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Solopreneurship, despite its name, is anything but a solo pursuit. As we find success in our agency work, we inevitably need to build a team that can help us serve our clients and expand our footprint.

As MVRK, my CRM strategy and implementation consulting agency, starts its seventh fiscal year, I’m very happy to say that my team is now composed of seven individuals who operate from six different countries. What’s more, none of us live in the three countries where we mainly do business (USA, Canada and the UK).

I have hired each of the individuals who are on the team myself. And I discovered them in a unique but repeatable way. In this article, I’m going to review the method that I’ve used to build those relationships with potential talent and share how I’ve been able to make them a part of my team. All with zero dollars spent.

For the first three years of running my business, I operated fully solo. But as I started to build success, I had an important realization: The clients that enjoyed working with me did not want to leave.

One of the projects that I worked on in my early years was implementing an entire Salesforce CRM system from the ground up for a Philippines-based recruitment agency. This agency was staffing talent in North America, so I knew I had a connection I could leverage to find that initial team member.

I defined the requirements, and that recruitment agency put some talent in front of me. From there, I selected somebody who I felt was going to work. I believe that I got quite lucky with my first hire because that individual is still a member of my team.

While I support the recruitment agency model and believe it works for many companies, the reality is that an agency is still a middleman that does not add a tremendous amount of value.  In my case, eventually, the individual in question wanted to continue working with me, without having to go through the agency. As a result, we formed a relationship directly.

Of course, it’s important to check any terms of service that you’ve signed before you make this kind of transition. But using an agency is not the only option. There is a way that you can leverage remote talent without relying on the offshore recruiting industry. It’s a little bit more work, but it’s a lot more rewarding for both you and the talent that you hire.

As we come to the end of 2026 and move towards 2027, you need to realize that relying on talent only in your immediate geographic area is limiting your ability to grow. Except for industries where in-person presence is required for regulatory or delivery purposes, there is no reason why you should limit yourself to hiring people in your city, in your state or province, or in your country.

This world is big, and there’s talent to be found in a lot more places than just your backyard. The best way that I have found to discover that talent is to go to the online communities where they hang out, share their knowledge and build a network. Crucially, these are also the places where they can discover you without tremendous costs.

I have found Reddit in particular is an incredible source of talent. What’s more, I haven’t spent a single dollar on advertising job ads or on recruiter fees. I’ve been able to build those relationships myself. Reddit has various communities, many that are specifically niched to your industry, and it is those places where individuals from across the world are hanging out.

To find talent via Reddit communities, I’ve built simple intake forms asking the right questions to vet individuals. Forget about asking for resumes. Instead, my process is simple. I share a request for talent in a relevant community, ensuring I follow the rules of that community. Within that request, I ask people to fill in my form as a first step. This gives me everything I need to find individuals who look like the best potential options and invite them for an interview.

From here, I vet them using the standard process and offer extended initial term contracts to those who are a good fit. Extended initial term contracts are ideal in this situation. They allow you to extend the term if you find you work together effectively, but also provide a clean separation if things don’t work out.

As you can see, there’s no need to pay somebody else to find talent for you. For many solopreneurs, this is a waste of money and time. Instead, go to relevant online communities (Reddit is just one option) where those individuals hang out, build real relationships with them and hire the right people for your team. It’s a valuable route to solopreneur success.

#5493. Current price of oil as of November 9, 2026

As of 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil sold for $97.65 per barrel (using Brent as the benchmark, which we’ll get into momentarily). That’s $2.66 lower than yesterday and approximately a $33.50 rise over the past year.

It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly.

When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups.

Still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”).

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer—more of an immediate relief to assist the consumer and keep critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Oil and natural gas are both major energy fuels. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible—which increases demand for natural gas.

When examining oil’s performance, there are generally two major benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5492. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.
