#5490. Your Business May Be Invisible to AI. Here Are 7 Simple Fixes You Can Make This Week.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Learn how to improve AI visibility with seven practical website, content and credibility fixes that help customers discover and evaluate your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Imagine a prospect asking an AI assistant to recommend a business in your category. Three competitors appear. Yours does not. You have a functioning website, years of experience and a steady stream of content. Yet the customer never learns you exist.

That scenario is worth investigating, but not because AI has a single secret ranking formula. Different tools generate different responses. Some retrieve live web pages; others depend on a combination of search results and existing knowledge. A recommendation can change with the question, location, timing and context. One test is not proof that your business is universally invisible.

The real opportunity is simpler. Make it easier for a person, a search engine and an AI-powered discovery tool to understand exactly what you offer, who benefits and what evidence supports your claims. You can begin with seven manageable improvements, many of which strengthen traditional search and conversions at the same time.

Start with customer language, not marketing jargon. If you sell cybersecurity services to banks, someone may ask, “Who helps regional banks prepare for a security audit?” They are less likely to type your carefully crafted positioning statement. Your first job is to understand the questions that occur before a buying decision.

Write five to 10 realistic prompts from sales calls, customer emails and proposal requests. Include a category question, a problem question, a comparison question and one that names your market. Test them in more than one AI search experience. Record the date, precise wording, companies mentioned, cited sources and whether your own website is among those sources.

Keep branded prompts separate. “Tell me about Acme Consulting” checks brand recognition; “Which firms can improve manufacturing supply-chain forecasting?” investigates discovery by an unfamiliar buyer. Confusing the two creates false confidence.

Your 20-minute action: Create a spreadsheet with columns for prompt, platform, date, cited source, competitor and opportunity. Treat observations as directional research, not an audited visibility score. Repeat the same prompt set monthly to look for persistent patterns.

Too many homepages use language that could describe any company: “We unlock transformational growth through next-generation solutions.” It sounds sophisticated but leaves a buyer wondering what is actually for sale. If a customer cannot understand the offer in ten seconds, that is a messaging problem long before it becomes a technical SEO problem.

Replace abstraction with a simple structure: “We help [specific audience] solve [specific problem] through [specific product or service], so they can [realistic outcome].” For example: “We help multi-location clinics improve patient acquisition and appointment conversion through search, content and website optimization.”

Then add proof nearby: industries served, a concrete capability, a customer example or a documented credential. Do not paste an entire keyword list into your opening paragraph. Make the first 100 words accurate, readable and specific, with one primary H1 that matches the subject of the page.

Your 20-minute action: Ask someone outside your organization to read the first screen of your homepage. Can they explain whom you serve, what you deliver and what action to take next? If not, rewrite it before investing in additional content.

Businesses often publish broad thought leadership but hide the details a buyer needs: price ranges, implementation steps, eligibility, limitations and alternatives. That leaves both customers and answer-generating systems with incomplete information.

Ask sales and customer-service teams which questions recur immediately before someone books a meeting or requests a quote. Select five. Build accurate answers into the relevant service or product pages, not a disconnected wall of generic FAQs. Use a descriptive H2 question and answer it directly in the first sentence, followed by examples, constraints and the next decision a buyer needs to make.

If pricing varies, explain the variables rather than inventing a price. If delivery timelines depend on approvals, say so. If the product is not suitable for every customer, acknowledge that explicitly. Useful answers increase confidence because they reduce uncertainty, not because they repeat a search phrase.

This approach aligns with a broader shift toward commercially useful content. For additional perspective, Entrepreneur has covered how businesses can earn leads across both AI search and conventional Google discovery.

Your 45-minute action: Publish one complete answer on each of your top five revenue-driving pages. Review the result on mobile. Does a buyer get the information without opening an accordion, guessing terminology or scheduling a sales call?

“Trusted,” “innovative” and “industry-leading” are not proof. Any competitor can make the same claims. Instead, help a skeptical prospect verify what you say. That might mean a named subject-matter expert, clear methodology, customer references with consent, original observations, dated research, documented product features or a candid case study.

An effective case study explains the initial problem, what changed, how success was measured and what the outcome means. A claimed 300% improvement without a baseline is less persuasive than a transparent account of the metric, time period and relevant limitations. Not every business can disclose client names, but permissioned or anonymized evidence can still be useful if presented accurately.

For expertise-led services, include author credentials, an updated bio and an explanation of who is responsible for the advice. For regulated industries, prioritize accurate, appropriately reviewed content over speed.

Your 30-minute action: Select your most profitable service page and add one piece of verifiable evidence plus a short explanation of why it matters to the buyer. Then identify what proof is still missing.

You can write a perfect page and undermine it with a noindex directive, a broken canonical tag, restrictive robots rules or weak internal linking. Start by checking the pages that generate or could generate revenue. Avoid treating technical optimization as a giant sitewide project when a focused inspection of five pages will reveal practical priorities.

Use Google Search Console to inspect indexing and important search queries. Confirm that key page content is present as readable text, accessible from relevant navigation and consistent with its title and meta description. Structured data can support eligible search features when it accurately represents visible content, but no special schema guarantees inclusion in AI answers.

Google’s official guidance for generative AI search reinforces that strong SEO foundations and distinctive, useful content remain central. There is no requirement to purchase a special AI markup package.

If you want public pages eligible for inclusion in ChatGPT Search, examine bot-access policies too. OpenAI distinguishes its search crawler from other crawlers, so site owners should review the current documentation rather than assuming all AI bot traffic serves the same purpose.

Your 30-minute action: Inspect five commercially important URLs for index eligibility, broken links, visible text and relevant internal links. Assign each issue to a named owner with a completion date.

A website is necessary, but it is also a controlled channel. Buyers often validate a company through independent sources, including industry associations, credible media, customer reviews, professional directories and expert participation. Those sources are valuable because they can corroborate facts, not because a business purchased a large volume of mentions.

Start with accuracy: Is your business name consistent? Are leaders and services described correctly? Are your credentials up to date? Can a customer find substantive contributions rather than a directory entry alone? Then focus on places that matter in your market. A healthcare founder may benefit more from a recognized professional association or reputable sector publication than a generic syndication network.

Entrepreneur has also examined the role of credible outside recognition in a changing search environment. The practical lesson is to earn citations and mentions through work worth referencing rather than mechanically distributing the same press release everywhere.

Your 45-minute action: Correct three important third-party profiles, then identify one legitimate opportunity to contribute an original data point, expert explanation or customer insight to an industry publication.

It is tempting to turn AI visibility into a single number. But being named frequently does not guarantee revenue, and AI answers are inconsistent enough that screenshots are a weak stand-alone measurement system. Separate the signals you can observe from the outcomes your organization actually needs.

Track whether your brand appears for a consistent set of buyer questions. Record citations where platforms expose them. Review identifiable AI referral traffic in analytics, but recognize that some journeys will not carry an obvious referral label. Combine those indicators with form submissions, qualified meetings, pipeline and revenue. Ask new prospects how they discovered you, while understanding that self-reported attribution is imperfect.

For leadership reporting, a simple monthly scorecard beats a glossy dashboard that cannot explain its methodology. Show changes to priority pages, visible search and referral trends, sales opportunities and what you plan to test next. Make it clear which trends are observed, estimated or unavailable.

Your 30-minute action: Establish a baseline this month and choose one commercial metric to improve. A rise in citations may be encouraging; a rise in qualified opportunities is the outcome the business can use.

Do not confuse a seven-day implementation sprint with seven-day rankings. Search systems can take time to discover and process changes. Results depend on competition, platform behavior, website quality and the strength of your evidence. The point of the sprint is to eliminate obvious weaknesses and create a defensible plan.

AI search has changed the way some buyers research providers, but it has not removed the need for fundamentals. A clear offer, useful answers, accessible pages, credible evidence and disciplined measurement improve the experience for the human buyer first. They also give discovery systems more accurate material to work with.

The question for business owners is not, “How do I trick AI into recommending me?” It is, “Have I given customers and credible sources enough useful information to understand why my company belongs on the shortlist?” That is a much more productive place to begin.

For organizations that want to examine these issues more systematically, I use an AI visibility assessment approach through Bullzeye Media Marketing’s GEO practice. The same starting principle applies whether you work with an advisor or manage it internally: Diagnose the gaps before spending on execution.

Imagine a prospect asking an AI assistant to recommend a business in your category. Three competitors appear. Yours does not. You have a functioning website, years of experience and a steady stream of content. Yet the customer never learns you exist.

That scenario is worth investigating, but not because AI has a single secret ranking formula. Different tools generate different responses. Some retrieve live web pages; others depend on a combination of search results and existing knowledge. A recommendation can change with the question, location, timing and context. One test is not proof that your business is universally invisible.

The real opportunity is simpler. Make it easier for a person, a search engine and an AI-powered discovery tool to understand exactly what you offer, who benefits and what evidence supports your claims. You can begin with seven manageable improvements, many of which strengthen traditional search and conversions at the same time.

#5489. Bain Capital’s Ajay Agarwal bet on robots when Silicon Valley wouldn’t. Now he sees a ‘golden era’ for physical AI

Morgan Chittum here. The point of venture capital? Get in early on the next big thing. But when one firm backs a buzzy startup, others often rush to follow. The more compelling—albeit riskier—story belongs to the contrarian: the investor willing to get there first and stand alone.

That’s the kind of bet Bain Capital Ventures’ Ajay Agarwal made more than two decades ago, backing a robotics startup that Silicon Valley investors had largely turned away. The company was Kiva Systems, which Amazon would later acquire for $775 million.

When Agarwal met Kiva cofounder Mick Mountz in 2004, the company had no revenue, no finished product, and no customers. At the time, software was a quicker, cheaper route to market. But Mountz’s pitch was simple: Instead of making warehouse workers walk the aisles to retrieve products, have robots bring the shelves to them. “Within five minutes of the meeting with Mick, I thought to myself, ‘This is the best meeting I’ve been in in 18 months,’” Agarwal told me. “I didn’t know anything about robotics or hardware, but he explained the problem in a way that you could explain it to your grandmother.”

Convincing Bain’s partners to invest, however, would take more work. “Their initial reaction, which I don’t blame them for, was ‘We don’t know anything about robots,’” Agarwal said.

Through Bain’s network, Agarwal connected Kiva’s team with Don Ralph, who ran North American e-commerce fulfillment for Staples, for additional due diligence. That one-hour meeting turned into three. The next day, Ralph called Agarwal: “I’ve been in this industry for 35 years. That was the single most compelling technology I’ve ever seen. You have to invest.”

Bain later led Kiva’s first funding round and Staples became its first customer. High-profile companies like Zappos, Gap, and Zara followed suit. Eight years later, Amazon bought it for $775 million. Bain told Fortune its initial investment in Kiva generated a 26.6-fold return.

Now, Agarwal sees an even bigger, wider opportunity. “We’re in the golden age of hardware and physical AI,” he said. That’s the technology that lets robots and other machines perceive and act in the real world.

This time, though, the rest of Silicon Valley has joined in.

Robotics and physical AI startups raised $27.6 billion in funding across 1,009 deals in 2025, more than double the previous year’s total, according to PitchBook figures. Among them is TerraFirma, a construction robotics company that Bain was the first to back in 2024. In July, the startup announced a $100 million Series A led by Kleiner Perkins, with Bain investing again.

What makes Agarwal think this momentum will last? For starters, the talent. TerraFirma’s founders, Noah Schochet and Noah McGuinness, came from SpaceX. Physical Intelligence, another leading robotics startup, was started by Berkeley roboticist Sergey Levine and ex-Google DeepMind researcher Karol Hausman.

“I think it’s a reaction a little bit to people feeling jaded by 20 years of workflow software,” Agarwal said. “People may be feeling like this is not ambitious enough. I want to do something bigger. I want to do something harder.”

The hardware is also cheaper. Many crucial components now cost a fraction of what they did years ago. Part of that comes down to scale: Smartphone and electric vehicle makers buy up cameras, sensors, and batteries in massive quantities, helping drive down the cost of parts that robots use as well. “That means the ROI that you can deliver is so much more compelling,” he said.

Finally, more advanced AI means machines have a better shot at handling real-world scenarios. “They can deal with situations they haven’t seen before,” Agarwal said. “They can adapt and adjust to the edge cases which inevitably happen in a physical environment.”

Twenty-two years ago, Agarwal had to convince his partners to take robots seriously. That’s no longer the hard part. It’s finding a bet the rest of Silicon Valley hasn’t already crowded into.

#5488. The CEO job is hard enough to land once. HP’s incoming chief has done it twice

Emma Walmsley is joining an exclusive club. When she takes over HP in January, the former GSK chief will become a two-time CEO of a major multinational, having crossed three industries to get there.

Her trajectory offers a revealing study in how executives build careers that make them attractive to boards across industries.

Walmsley spent 17 years at L’Oréal, holding management positions across four global cities before running its consumer products business in China. She joined GSK in 2010, became CEO of its consumer healthcare division in 2015, and took the top job in 2017, becoming the first woman to lead a major pharmaceutical company.

Over nearly nine years, she navigated activist pressure, the pandemic, and the separation of Haleon, GSK’s consumer healthcare company. She also faced investor criticism over GSK’s drug pipeline and shareholder returns. Since 2019, she has served on Microsoft’s board, gaining exposure to the technology industry and a company central to HP’s PC business.

Her appointment follows the departure of Enrique Lores, who rose from engineering intern to CEO during more than three decades at HP before leaving for PayPal in February. After nine months under interim chief Bruce Broussard, HP has chosen a leader whose career followed a strikingly different trajectory.

Her next assignment presents a different commercial challenge.

HP says it needs to unlock growth as AI transforms personal computing. Analysts see more immediate pressures. Rising memory-chip prices are squeezing manufacturers, PC demand faces uncertainty, and the printing business continues to contract.

Walmsley joins a prominent group of executives recruited for another turn in the corner office. Kraft Heinz appointed former Kellanova chief Steve Cahillane in 2026. Verizon tapped former PayPal CEO Dan Schulman in 2025. Starbucks recruited Chipotle chief Brian Niccol in 2024, while Papa John’s hired former Wendy’s CEO Todd Penegor the same year. Mary Dillon, who previously led U.S. Cellular and Ulta Beauty, became Foot Locker’s CEO in 2022.

Their appointments reflect the appeal of executives with established track records running large organizations, navigating competitive pressures, and leading corporate transformations.

According to Spencer Stuart, 21% of incoming S&P 1500 CEOs in 2024 had previously led a public company, up eight percentage points over three years.

But hiring repeat CEOs comes with a revealing complication. In a study of 855 S&P 500 CEOs, Spencer Stuart found that 70% of those who went on to lead another S&P 500 company delivered stronger market-adjusted shareholder returns in their first CEO role. Researchers warned that experienced CEOs can rely too heavily on familiar strategies.

For Walmsley, whose experience restructuring GSK helped establish her credentials, HP presents a test of how readily those skills transfer to a technology business confronting different competitive pressures.

#5487. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5486. HR leaders have a new nightmare: Job seekers asking ChatGPT what employees really think of their company

HR leaders have a new fear: Job candidates asking ChatGPT what their company is really like.

Some 70% of job seekers now use generative AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Perplexity to research employers, new Indeed data shows. And when job seekers ask about company culture, roughly 40% of the sources cited come from Glassdoor and Indeed, not company career pages.

That creates a new challenge for HR. AI is helping shape candidates’ perceptions of employers using information companies don’t directly control. A polished career page may tell one story, while employee reviews tell another—and job seekers can ask a chatbot to piece it all together.

But AI isn’t uncovering anything that isn’t already online, says Taylor Meadows, principal advisor at Glassdoor. His advice is to feed the beast.

“Your employer brand exists whether you are participating in it or not,” Meadows says. He recommends starting with an AI audit, asking different LLMs, “What is it like to work at X company?” Then, “reverse engineer” the problems that surface.

Meadows also suggests publishing Q&As addressing real questions from employees and candidates on social media and third-party review sites. “Let that be the good, the bad, and the ugly,” he says. “It’s going to be an opportunity for you to talk about what’s going well, but then it’s going to also be an opportunity to exercise some humility.”

Companies should also create content that showcases what it’s like to work in different departments, since culture can vary by team. Encouraging employees to share authentic experiences helps, too, Meadows says.

Even offboarding matters. Departing employees may leave reviews that AI later surfaces, making their final impression of the company especially important.

“None of this is about perfection and none of this is about control,” Meadows says. “It’s just about informing and influencing.”

Kristin StollerEditorial Director, Fortune Live Mediakristin.stoller@fortune.com

This week, Sabrina Clark, chief people officer at leadership consultancy SYPartners, answers your burning workplace questions. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Q: A friend of mine received strong performance reviews from three previous managers at their company. Then they got a new manager who put them on a PIP (performance improvement plan). They could not switch back to working with one of their previous managers because they were on a PIP, and their new manager didn’t indicate when it would end.

Because a competing company was interested in this employee, they chose to leave and join that company, but is there anything they could have done if they wanted to stay at their previous employer?

A: I imagine your friend is pretty frustrated to have gone from being rated a strong performer to being put on a PIP. While the discrepancy might lie with their new manager, it’s also possible their previous managers avoided giving difficult feedback or that the demands of your friend’s new work environment exposed gaps in their skills.

Whatever the reason, I would have advised your friend to ask their new manager, “What would success look like, and when will we assess it?” A performance improvement plan should always specify what needs to improve and how progress will be assessed, and include a timeline with regular check-ins and a defined review date. It should also explain the possible outcomes: successful completion, an extension with a new review date, or termination. Your friend deserved to know where the finish line was.

Given the seemingly strained relationship with the new manager, your friend could also have involved an HR leader or the manager’s manager to help uncover why their reviews differed so much and to help decide what happens next.

Ultimately, your friend could have pressed for more clarity, but their employer owed them a clear and fair path forward.

#5485. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX have joined a growing list of companies rejecting OKXICE tokenized stocks trading platform, bringing the total objections to 67. The update added Palantir, S&P Global, KLA, Super Micro Computer and Meta to the list. That puts 56 of the 62 companies originally selected for the platform among those objecting to their shares being traded through the proposed venue.

OKX–ICE Stock Venue’s Issuer Objections Reach 62Boeing and ServiceNow have raised objections to the venture’s proposed symbols, leaving eight of the 63 originally proposed symbols without a disclosed opt-out.⚠️ Personal market analysis only. NFA — manage risk and DYOR.… pic.twitter.com/CXjQRpQOnH

The development comes as Musk recently attracted attention for responding to a separate ICE-backed Hyperliquid initiative. The billionaire replied “Interesting” to investor Stanley Druckenmiller’s October 29 announcement about investing in Trade[XYZ], which is partnering with ICE to bring Hyperliquid-based perpetual futures to US markets.

The growing opposition presents a significant obstacle for OKXICE tokenized stocks plan, a joint venture between cryptocurrency exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange, the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange.

The proposed platform aims to bring tokenised versions of US stocks onto blockchain infrastructure, allowing investors to trade around the clock using stablecoins such as USDC. But companies have increasingly exercised their right to prevent unaffiliated platforms from offering tokenised versions of their shares.

Tesla and SpaceX appeared in OKX-ICE’s November 2 notice alongside Amazon, Netflix, Lam Research and SoFi Technologies. Subsequent updates pushed the total number of objecting companies to 67 by today.

The original selection included 62 companies covering 63 proposed stock tickers. The latest tally therefore extends beyond the initial roster, with 56 original companies having filed objections.

Under the SEC’s temporary Innovation Exemption, trading venues must notify companies before offering third-party tokenised versions of their shares. Issuers can object within 30 days, preventing the venue from listing those particular tokenised shares.

Importantly, these objections do not represent a blanket rejection of tokenisation. Companies can still explore their own tokenisation arrangements or participate through other venues.

OKXICE tokenized stocks proposal uses permissioned liquidity pools on OKX’s X Layer blockchain, with Uniswap v4 infrastructure supporting trading. Investors would undergo identity and sanctions checks before accessing the platform.

The initiative aims to combine blockchain settlement with extended trading hours, although the growing number of objections raises questions about which major stocks could eventually become available.

#5483. The crypto world braces for Liz Warren’s return. Has anything changed?

She’s back. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the longtime scourge of the crypto industry, is poised to return as a political force in January. That’s when Warren is expected to take over as Chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee—a role that is critical for steering financial legislation, and comes with broad subpoena and investigative power. This is not exactly good news for crypto firms, of course. The question, though, is whether—just maybe—Warren and the industry can lay aside old antagonisms in order to advance both consumer protection and financial innovation.

As background, the bad blood between Warren and the crypto industry stems from the Biden years. That’s when former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler set out to basically extinguish the U.S. crypto industry with a spate of lawsuits and investigations. Among Washington D.C. insiders, many saw Warren and her staffers as the architects of Gensler’s campaign.

In response to that Biden-era legal onslaught, the crypto industry overcame its longtime disdain of Washington politics, and it waged a big-money campaign in 2024 to elect President Trump, and to drive critics from Congress. The campaign worked stunningly well. Crypto firms helped sweep Trump into office, leading to a hands-off regulatory environment that left Warren fuming ineffectively on the sidelines.

Now, the shoe is on the other foot again. Despite blowing around $170 million on campaign ads to boost Republican candidates in the midterms, the crypto industry had what one lobbyist described simply as an “awful night.” Not only did crypto firms fail to do anything to stop the Democrats’ blue wave, they made tactical choices that look downright foolish in hindsight. That includes spending over $63 million in a failed bid to defeat crypto skeptic Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who not only won his Senate race by a comfortable margin, but will likely become Chair of the Agriculture Committee, which oversees commodities regulation.

When they are wielding committee gavels next January (which is widely expected but not confirmed), don’t expect Warren and Brown to do the crypto industry any favors. But it doesn’t necessarily follow that we’ll see a return to the scorched earth tactics of the Biden years. Ron Hammond, Head of Policy at Wintermute, notes that a recent Time essay by Warren appeared to telegraph her agenda. The essay puts CEOs of various industries on notice and promises to target Trump family corruption, but makes no mention at all of crypto—potentially a sign the industry will not be an immediate target.

Hammond, who is deeply plugged into the D.C. crypto scene, also noted that the crypto firms that stand to lose the most from Warren’s return are those that are seeking out or have obtained banking charters. In this scenario, Warren may ally with traditional banks, which earlier this year helped smother the Clarity Act, in order to block or roll back those charters.

Warren and her allies will be unable to make any drastic moves, though, because the Trump-appointed heads of key financial agencies—including the SEC, CFTC, and OCC—will hold their positions until the end of his term. This means that, for the next year or two, we can expect moves by Warren that are symbolic in nature, but that point to where she and the Democratic Party are heading in 2028.

Politics is never static, and while it’s a safe bet that Warren is not going to become a Bitcoin HODLer, there is a world where the Senator becomes less antagonistic. As an olive branch, she could acknowledge the undeniable benefits of blockchain innovations like stablecoins, as well as the popularity of crypto among younger Americans.

As for the crypto industry, the midterm results delivered a long overdue lesson that politics in Washington D.C. is a long game and that, while trying to bludgeon critics with PAC money may feel satisfying, it’s not the most effective strategy. And while crypto CEOs will never see eye-to-eye with Liz Warren—their respective libertarian and progressive worldviews are simply too different—there is room to acknowledge her advocacy for consumers is sincere, even if it is at times misguided.

Maybe all of this is naive, but last week’s election results felt like a break from politics as usual. Voters appear exhausted by jerks on both the left and the right and, for now at least, moderation is the order of the day. How refreshing would it be if Liz Warren and the crypto industry came to recognize that too?

#5482. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5481. Jensen Huang’s $21 billion net worth at stake: CEO’s admission of affair with an alleged Chinese spy is ‘capping gains’ for Nvidia stock

For the first time in a long time, Nvidia’s investors may be feeling a little cold about their investment’s performance. Last week, the famed chipmaker and many of its peers in the wider AI and technology industry suffered an estimated $2.5 trillion rout as investors questioned the hurdles facing the sector. The issue is political: The midterms saw Democrats win the Senate, the House, and many statehouses, prompting the question of whether regulation will become more complex under a divided government.But adding to Nvidia investors’ concerns is the admission of its CEO, Jensen Huang, that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang’s net worth, tied to the computer processor and AI company he co-founded, stood at just over $171 billion early last week. It dropped to $150.9 billion by Thursday, and briefly rebounded to $154.9 billion by Friday—the latest data point on Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

The trajectory follows the path of Nvidia’s share price, now down 18.6% in the past month.

But even as signs of a small reversal bloomed Friday, the weekend brought another blow. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a statement shared overnight.

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA … you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility,” he added, saying he would work to “earn back” the confidence of the board, partners and company shareholders.

The woman he had an affair with has been identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board of directors confirmed in an accompanying statement overnight that it had launched an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The Chinese government has denied involvement in the alleged spy plot involving Huang, calling the debacle “nothing but smears.”

The board added that while it has no reason to believe sensitive national security or NVIDIA “secrets” were compromised, it will “examine all available information.”

Analysts are digesting the news this morning ahead of markets opening in New York. Equities in Asia rallied this morning, noted Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid, “although concerns surrounding an internal investigation involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are capping gains.”

“The company is down around -3.5% on platforms that provide weekend prices,” he added.

The importance of Nvidia among the companies at the forefront of AI development cannot be overstated. It is the premier supplier of chips to AI companies and one of the largest investors and guarantors of companies in the AI supply chain—to the tune of hundreds of billions.

Yet President Trump was unruffled when asked about one of the country’s most famous CEOs being potentially implicated in a national security threat.

“I have not spoken to [Huang] about it,” Trump told reporters last night. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”

Betting on the prediction market Kalshi had the odds of Huang leaving the company before July 27 at 25%. Professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, put the odds of his resignation at 50-50. Huang owns the largest single stake in Nvidia, and his children are among his employees. If he were to leave, there is no obvious successor.

Nvidia’s board said it has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

President Trump was also confident Huang would continue to lead the company, saying: “He’s done an amazing job for our country.”

#5480. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5479. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5478. ‘The nail that sticks out gets hammered first’: Elon Musk’s net worth falls $113 billion from Tesla and SpaceX drops

Wall Street had a historic moment the day after Democrats swept the midterms, with the Dow rising 3% on Wednesday, its best performance after a midterm in 44 years. But on Thursday, it erased those gains, dropping 2.9% as investors dumped AI-related stocks like AMD and Micron.

But for Elon Musk, who spent an estimated $427.5 million to $483 million on backing Republicans, the losses started on the same day as the rally, and then accelerated. Tesla shares fell by 3.3% and SpaceX shares fell by 3.8% on Wednesday’s market close, erasing tens of billions from Musk’s fortune as they also underperformed against the S&P 500’s 1.6% growth and stocks like Amazon and Apple, which jumped 6.1% and 5.3%, per Fortune’s analysis. He lost $33.5 billion of his paper wealth that day, and another $79.7 billion in Thursday’s selloff, bringing his two-day loss to about $113 billion as of market close on Nov. 5, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

In short, in 48 hours, Tesla and SpaceX went from having a combined market cap of about $3.5 trillion on Tuesday night, to a combined $3.04 trillion on Thursday night, wiping out about $456 billion in total. As of Thursday night, SpaceX’s market cap is $1.68 trillion, about 87% of what it was on midterms night, and Tesla’s market cap is $1.36 trillion, about 86% of its value from then.

Investors are worried the two companies and their founder will face increased scrutiny from the new Congress. Democrats have signaled they want to investigate Musk’s involvement with DOGE gutting federal agencies and his potential conflicts of interests, since SpaceX has earned billions from federal contracts. The incoming House Oversight Committee chair Rep. Robert Garcia has vowed to investigate “corporate corruption,” and his spokesperson told Politico on Oct. 20 that Musk’s role in DOGE “is something we plan to investigate.”

“The nail that sticks out gets hammered first, and Musk has certainly stuck out, especially in government, whether it be donations, the election, and any of the feathers he ruffled while he was at DOGE,” Keith Snyder, senior equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Fortune.

The scrutiny could extend to SpaceX’s satellite business, its most consistently profitable segment. Sen. Richard Blumenthal from Connecticut sent a letter to Musk asking about SpaceX’s contracts with the Department of Defense and its ability to restrict Starlink after reports circulated that Ukraine’s military lost access to Starlink without notice.

But Snyder said the brief SpaceX and Tesla selloff was investors having a “knee-jerk reaction” to the election and overestimating the impact Democrats can have on the companies. After all, President Donald Trump still has veto power over any major AI restrictions they can pass, and is still friendly toward Musk.

“Reining in AI has been a stated goal of theirs, but you have to remember Trump seems to still be backing Musk and has veto power,” Snyder said.

For investors hanging their hopes on a SpaceX and Tesla merger and worried about Democrats’ interference there, Snyder said that because the Federal Communications Commission has a Republican majority, he doesn’t expect major actions there except Democrats’ power to “dramatically slow things down.” Fortune has reported that the merger math doesn’t add up for SpaceX shareholders.

“There’s too many pieces that are already in place for Musk, for Tesla, for SpaceX that will allow him to continue without having to worry about any kind of Democratic action,” he said.

Some analysts take a more bearish stance. Dan Ives wrote in a note on Thursday that a Tesla SpaceX merger “faces a much tougher regulatory roadmap” because of Texas turning blue. This new political reality partially made possible by voters angry over data centers coincides with investors’ long-running concerns about the AI buildout being unsustainable. Snyder said that anxiety could’ve contributed to the SpaceX selloff, but that SpaceX has an advantage in already having broken ground on data centers.

On its Q3 earnings call before the midterms, Musk said he was confident the company can bring 10 gigawatts of compute online by 2027 on top of the 2.5 to 3 gigawatts SpaceX will have by the end of 2026, a total number that AI and semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis quantified as equivalent to all of Google’s data center capacity from 1999 to 2026 in just one and a half years.

“Even if they’re able to achieve 25% to 50% of that goal, that would be incredible in terms of capacity build out,” Snyder said.

He said where he sees more risk for SpaceX and for AI in general is if there’s a Democrat win in the White House in two years, since for now there will be a political gridlock with a Republican president and a Democrat-controlled Congress.

“The fears to these AI companies are real now,” he said. “[Democrats’] agenda has clearly stated they want to rein in AI, and so, ‘27, ‘28 is gonna be a stalemate, but it then becomes what happens in ‘29.”

#5477. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5476. Tight Budget? This Familiar Destination Could Help You Cut Expenses.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

With less room in their budgets, people are turning to a familiar resource they may have overlooked.

Shoppers looking to cut costs are rediscovering an old favorite location in their neighborhoods: their local library.

According to a new report from NPR, consumers are returning to the library to get more without stretching their paychecks.

One avid reader, Izzy Rivera, picks up at least one book a week from local libraries near her residence in Topeka, Kansas. She said in an interview with NPR that it “just isn’t realistic” for her to regularly buy new books as she saves up for law school.

Rivera checks out both physical books and digital ones through the Libby library app. She isn’t ruling out buying books altogether. Last month, she went to her local library’s used book sale and bought 15 books for around $20.

There are other instances where the library provided Rivera with free or low-cost materials. For example, she watches movies on the streaming app Kanopy, which requires a library card or university login.

Her library card also provides her with free access to The New York Times online, a perk that extends beyond her neighborhood. For example, The New York Public Library began offering visitors free access to The New York Times in January if they accessed the digital newspaper while on the library’s Wi-Fi network.

Rivera said she spends a lot of time at her local library.

“It’s somewhere I can go where I’m not expected to spend money,” she said. “If I were to go to a coffee shop just to get out and do something, the expectation would be to buy a coffee, even though I probably didn’t want a coffee.”

Librarians and library-goers across the country told NPR that financial pressures are drawing consumers into libraries. The pattern is familiar to library staff: When money gets tight, demand for their services grows.

Americans are cutting spending on optional items as they try to afford the necessities. A Pew Research Center report released last month found that 44% of Americans struggled to afford at least one basic necessity, like medical care or housing, over the previous year.

Meanwhile, 70% said they had trimmed spending on nonessentials like dining out and streaming subscriptions across the same time period. Pew Research conducted the survey in late August, and about 5,000 Americans responded.

Several of the nation’s largest public library systems showed NPR data reflecting recent increases in membership. More library-goers are also borrowing materials and attending events.

Maria McCauley, president of the American Library Association, said in an interview with NPR that she attributes some of that growth to “heightened awareness” of what libraries offer.

Libraries “are especially popular right now, I think, because people are aware that everything that we provide is free or very low cost,” McCauley said.

#5475. Current price of oil as of November 6, 2026

At 7:15 a.m. Eastern Time on November 6, 2026, oil was priced at $102.05 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s an increase of $2.53 compared with yesterday morning and around $38 higher than the price one year ago.

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.
