#5474. Your Customers Are Using AI Search. They’re Still Googling You, Too. Here’s What Your Marketing Strategy Might Be Missing.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A new audience-overlap finding is a useful corrective to the idea that AI search is replacing Google. And it changes how businesses should think about discovery and measurement.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I keep hearing a version of the same question from business leaders: Is AI search taking customers away from Google?

A new Similarweb audience-overlap figure offers a useful answer, with an important limit. In September, 93.7% of ChatGPT.com’s visitors also visited Google.com. The overlap ran the other way, too: 14.1% of Google.com’s visitors also visited ChatGPT.com, according to Search Engine Watch’s report.

That is not proof that someone asked ChatGPT about a product, then searched for it on Google. The data counts people who visited both websites during the month. It doesn’t show which one they used first, how often they searched, what they searched for or whether they bought anything. It also doesn’t capture the full use of either service through apps.

Those limits matter. But they don’t make the finding irrelevant. They tell us not to mistake channel overlap for channel substitution.

For years, marketers have organized discovery into tidy channels: search, social, referrals, paid media. AI assistants make that division harder to defend. A person might ask an AI tool to compare options, search a brand name in Google, watch a creator review, then visit a company’s site directly. The journey may cross several systems before the business gets a measurable click.

The Similarweb figure doesn’t prove that sequence. It does show why we shouldn’t assume that a visitor counted in an AI audience is a new person who has never used Google. Treating those groups as separate pools can lead to double-counting, inflated reach estimates and bad budget decisions.

I saw a version of this mistake when search was still new to many companies. Some treated SEO as a separate experiment instead of infrastructure for demand that already existed. The risk now is the reverse: treating AI discovery as a replacement for the search habits customers still have.

The better question isn’t which platform wins. It’s whether your brand is present, clear and credible when a customer moves between them.

The overlap stat also exposes a measurement problem. A customer might encounter a brand in an AI answer and later search for it by name. That later visit could show up as Google organic traffic, even if the earlier discovery helped create the demand. Or the AI interaction might never produce a visit at all. The audience-overlap data can’t tell us which happened.

That is why last-click reporting is a poor referee for this shift. A referral source can tell you where a session came from. It usually can’t tell you which earlier interactions made the brand worth looking up.

Google has begun giving site owners a clearer view of one part of the picture. Its Search Console generative AI performance report shows impressions for pages appearing in Google’s AI search features, including AI Overviews and AI Mode. That is useful visibility data, not proof of incremental traffic or revenue, and it doesn’t cover ChatGPT or other AI platforms.

Businesses should keep the measures separate. Track traditional search clicks, branded searches, qualified leads and sales. Alongside them, monitor which pages appear in Google’s AI features and whether your brand is cited in a consistent set of relevant AI prompts. Add a simple question to lead forms or post-purchase surveys: “Where did you first hear about us?” None of those signals proves, on its own, that AI caused a sale. Together, they can reveal patterns that last-click reports miss.

The response isn’t to split the marketing budget evenly between Google and AI. It’s to stop planning as if every platform reaches a different customer.

Keep investing in the parts of search that help customers find and evaluate you. Make sure the pages that explain your products, pricing and value are current. Understand which questions bring qualified prospects to your site. Then extend the same discipline to AI discovery: Check whether answer engines describe your business accurately, cite useful sources and include you when customers compare options.

Most importantly, connect the teams and dashboards. If SEO reports a decline in clicks while AI visibility rises, don’t declare one channel the winner and the other the loser. Look at branded search, lead quality, direct visits and conversion trends. Ask customers what influenced them. Compare the pattern over time, not just across one month’s traffic report.

I don’t read the 93.7% figure as evidence that Google is safe or that AI search is harmless to existing traffic. It doesn’t answer either question. I read it as a reason to be more precise: Customers can add a new way to discover a business without abandoning the old one.

Your customers may meet you in an AI answer and Google you before they act. The companies that understand both moments will make better decisions than the ones still asking which channel gets credit for the whole journey.

That is not proof that someone asked ChatGPT about a product, then searched for it on Google. The data counts people who visited both websites during the month. It doesn’t show which one they used first, how often they searched, what they searched for or whether they bought anything. It also doesn’t capture the full use of either service through apps.

#5473. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5472. How a Frenchman’s book on ‘Democracy in America’ nearly 200 years ago explains the midterms, from data centers to Texas

I turned to Alexis de Tocqueville, having read about him for years and never actually read him myself, after the Nov. 3 midterms handed Democrats a “blue tsunami” the likes of which I haven’t seen in my 43 years. Texas went blue down the line. And in 40 of 41 local votes across 10 states, Americans chose to limit data centers.

Within days, $3.2 trillion of AI-related stock market wealth was wiped out as investors bet the election winners would slow the AI buildout. Texas holds one-fifth of the planned data-center pipeline, and its governor-elect has promised to ban new approvals until the state legislature acts.

I had been privately skeptical, because data centers are the bedrock of the massive industrial boom powering most of America’s GDP growth. From an economic perspective, being anti-data center is like being pro-recession, I assumed, but Tocqueville’s Democracy in America explains a lot of what has really gone on in America for centuries.

Tocqueville was a young French aristocrat who toured the United States in 1831 and published Democracy in America in two volumes, dated 1835 and 1840. The Library of America calls it arguably “the most perceptive and influential book ever written about American politics and society.” One big idea he offered was what he called the “general equality of condition” among Americans, meaning how widely property and status were spread around. And this, he proposed, is the fact that the rest of American life comes out of. He argued that Americans hold tight to their property, care more about equality than liberty, and organize locally to get what they want. The data-center industry made its plans without accounting for any of that, and it’s an open question whether the Democrats who just won a landslide really understand it, themselves.

Most Gen Xers can barely remember a wave like this one. The closest historical comp is the 1974 blue wave that swept aside the corruption of the Nixon Watergate era. The 2026 midterms suggest a scrambling of the calculus of red states and blue states much like Donald Trump’s shocking election did a decade ago, when the “blue wall” of Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Michigan crumbled.

Nationally, Democrats have so far flipped seven Senate seats and are on track for at least 258 House seats. They took a majority of governors’ mansions for the first time since 2010, and Trump acknowledged that Democrats had secured both chambers. Down the ballot, voters in 10 states decided 41 local measures on data centers, and in 40 of the 41 they favored limits on development. In NBC’s exit poll, 76% said they would oppose a new data center in their community. There were many stunners, like Kansas electing its first Democratic senator since 1932, but Texas stands out as the signature shock.

The Lone Star state went blue across its statewide offices. Beyond the Senate and governor’s races, Democrats won agriculture commissioner, attorney general, land commissioner, comptroller, lieutenant governor and railroad commissioner. They have taken the state House for the first time since 2002. Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott and will be the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990, and the first ever Hispanic person to hold the office. The Texas House looks likely to have its first female and first Black speaker in the form of 87-year-old Senfronia Thompson, who took office in 1973.

Reading Tocqueville in this climate is downright spooky. He wrote in 1835 that American political bickering at first looks to a stranger “so incomprehensible and so puerile” that he can’t decide whether to pity the people or envy the happiness that lets them argue. I personally thought as much for months about the issue of data centers — a massively overstated environmental risk but a massively understated political and emotional issue — until voters proved they were not messing around.

Look closer, Tocqueville wrote, and nearly every faction of American political life comes down to one side trying “to limit,” and the other “to extend, the popular authority.” Five years later, in his second volume, he explained what made Americans different from the Europeans watching them. “The great advantage of the Americans is that they have arrived at a state of democracy without having to endure a democratic revolution; and that they are born equal, instead of becoming so.” Two centuries on, that birthright came out on Nov. 3 as a mass of voters told the Republican Party, and the data-center builders, something like “No, I don’t think so.”

Property, unlike aristocratic Europe where it is passed down from along family lines for centuries, is what keeps the whole thing from flying apart for most Americans, who are “possessed of sufficient property to desire the maintenance of order, yet not enough to excite envy.” Tocqueville observed that “the passions engendered by property are keenest and most tenacious amongst the middle classes.” And because equality leaves each person weak on his own, Americans band together to form what he called “associations,” without which they “become powerless if they do not learn voluntarily to help one another.”

Tocqueville also prophesied that Texas would hold the key to the American future. “The inhabitants of the United States are perpetually migrating to Texas, where they purchase land; and although they conform to the laws of the country, they are gradually founding the empire of their own language and their own manners,” he wrote, a decade before Texas joined the Union.

Texas has spent the 2020s proving him right. It added 391,243 residents in the year to July 2025, more than any other state for the third year in a row, reaching 31.7 million. It produced $2.9 trillion in GDP in 2025, and holds one-fifth of the planned 253-gigawatt data center pipeline nationwide. The five fastest-growing American cities, the Census Bureau revealed in May, were all in Texas, some for the second year running.

This year, Texas put every one of Tocqueville’s arguments on the ballot at once. Landowners fought transmission lines after a 2023 law cut the time regulators have to consider them from 365 days to 180. Groups like Save Rural Texas organized against data centers, and while Abbott ordered an audit of every data center in the grid queue, Hinojosa called for a statewide moratorium, vowing days before the vote to “stop the data center takeover.” Then the voters made clear in resounding fashion how they felt about property, equality and popular authority.

For a lot of voters this year, equality came down to the cost of living. In Gallup’s final preelection survey, 44% of voters called income and wealth distribution extremely important, the highest reading in the three midterms Gallup has measured it, up from 32% in 2018 and 31% in 2014. On PJM, the grid running from Illinois to New Jersey, the independent market monitor puts data centers at $6.3 billion of the latest auction’s $16.4 billion in capacity charges, and at $29.4 billion, or 46%, across the last four auctions. In the October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, 57% of Americans called home energy and utility costs unaffordable, up from 45% in February.

On property, Tocqueville wrote that “the heart of man is not so much caught by the undisturbed possession of anything valuable as by the desire, as yet imperfectly satisfied, of possessing it, and by the incessant dread of losing it.” The data-center fears, environmental concerns aside, cut straight to the American dread of losing one’s property. In August, a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found 57% of Texas voters opposed a data center in their community, including 43% of Republicans and 60% of rural voters. The other side claims property, too. Texas Policy Research, a free-market think tank, argues Texas should protect private property rights and free enterprise while making large electricity users pay the costs they impose on the grid.

The “associations” that Tocqueville observed were so obvious in this election season they hardly need mentioning. Data Center Watch, a tracker maintained by AI research firm 10a Labs, counted 833 opposition groups across 49 states by March 2026, up from 396 at the end of 2025. In June, Seattle’s city council voted unanimously for a one-year ban, making it the largest U.S. city to pass one. None of these ran through Washington.

Tocqueville spelled out the lesson in 1840: Americans describe their civic life in terms of self-interest. “The Americans… are fond of explaining almost all the actions of their lives by the principle of interest rightly understood,” he wrote. “They show with complacency how an enlightened regard for themselves constantly prompts them to assist each other.”

When they do something public-spirited, in other words, they insist it is in their own interest. They “seldom allow that they yield to emotions of this kind; they are more anxious to do honor to their philosophy than to themselves.” He didn’t mean that as an insult, calling the principle “the best suited of all philosophical theories to the wants of the men of our time,” and “their chief remaining security against themselves.”

That’s what most readings of the data-center fight, including mine, missed. From outside it looks like people guarding their power bills and their land. Others suspected the opposition was manufactured, even from China. The experts Fortune spoke to in June found it organic, with little evidence to support claims of China’s interference. The people in the fight talk about bills and property, as Tocqueville said they would, and they organized and voted in 41 places.

Americans misread themselves on the bigger question, too. Before the vote, fewer than half expected free and fair midterms, according to a University of California, San Diego, survey. Experts weren’t much sunnier. In Bright Line Watch’s October survey, their median forecast of a free and fair election was 75%, and one article in Political Science Quarterly argued the country had descended into soft competitive authoritarianism. But Tocqueville reasoned in the chapter “Why Great Revolutions Will Become More Rare” that a country of small owners has too much to lose to blow itself up.

“Nations are less disposed to make revolutions in proportion as personal property is augmented and distributed amongst them,” he wrote. Americans’ revolutions come through the ballot box when equality feels threatened. The contrast with Germany and France, where disaffected Gen Zers’ protests have turned violent in the streets, looks straight out of the late 18th century.

Democrats would be making a Tocqueville-sized mistake to read Nov. 3 as a conversion. The border counties that swung toward them had swung the other way two years earlier. In 2024, Trump won all four counties in the Rio Grande Valley, a region Democrats had swept in almost every presidential election since at least the 1920s. In Texas, where Democrats won their largest House majority since the 1993 session, several Democratic flips were decided by mere hundreds of votes. In Kansas, Hamilton won as an “independent-minded Democrat.” He avoided association with national Democrats and said he wouldn’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer for another leadership position, even though his campaign took $5 million from a PAC associated with Schumer.

The voters who elected them were following the bills, the land and the town meeting and will surely follow them again.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5471. How to Properly Lead a Team When the Founder Still Calls Every Shot

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Reporting to a founder is different from reporting to a manager. Here are four ways to make this special relationship work.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For more than a decade, founder-led companies have returned more than twice as much to shareholders as companies that are not founder-led, according to Bain. In tech, the multiple is higher still. The executives I speak with take roles at founder-led companies because they’re attracted to high returns. Then they discover the founder will not let go of the work the executive was hired to lead.

I coach C-suite executives who report to founders and co-founders, including COOs, CPOs, CTOs, chiefs of staff and heads of function. I also coach founders themselves, at companies ranging in size from a handful of employees to publicly traded behemoths. Most managing-up advice, my own included, assumes your boss holds a particular role, but this advice doesn’t stick when your founder is running a company they built themselves.

Every founder keeps a short list of tasks they will never hand over, no matter what the organizational chart says, and some of those tasks are likely on your job description.

I worked with a chief of staff who reported to a founder. In interviews and in their job description, they were told they would own strategy, operations and business development, but they quickly learned that they didn’t truly own them. Sure, they could have fought for the scope they were promised, but it would have been a losing battle. Instead, I coached them to focus on projects where they had real ownership.

Delegation can break down in the opposite direction, too. A COO I worked with ran board meetings but was never asked to manage board relationships or investor conversations. Her founder kept those tasks close to the vest. At the same time, he handed over responsibility for the entire budget to her and took little interest in even reviewing it. Through our coaching, she decided to loop him in more than he wanted and used the board meetings as a way to connect with board members and investors.

Ask your founder what they want to stay close to, then watch what happens over the next quarter. Ask again as the company scales, because the list will likely move. What a founder says they will hand over and what they actually hold onto are not always different.

Nearly every founder-led company has a small group of friends and peers whose input carries weight. They often look like co-founders, early employees, board members or an executive assistant who has been there since the start. In some cases, this group includes a family member with no formal ties to the company other than being related to the founder.

Over the years, I’ve coached clients to look far beyond the org chart when thinking about how to get things done. We spend sessions creating their own map of key individuals who influence the founder, both formally and informally.

In your first 90 days of a new job, it’s important to take special notice of whose wisdom your founder repeats and whose objection changes their mind. Build relationships with those people before you need them.

How a founder talks is often different from what they mean, and the translation depends on which type you are working with. I’ve seen two communication patterns come up repeatedly.

Visionary founders think out loud. They express a half-formed idea in a Monday meeting, but your team hears it as a mandate. They reprioritize their quarter unnecessarily around something the founder has already moved past, and your team ends up spending a weekend building a deck nobody asked for.

Conversely, operator founders speak in specifics. When they ask a passing question about a metric, your team should get to work and make sure they have the information they want. These founders mean what they say, and you need to listen.

In practice, this requires you to get clear on the type of founder you’re working with, as well as what they want from you and your team. You want to know whether an idea is just an idea that can stay half-formed or a real ask that requires action and follow-through. To find out, you need to ask directly.

Founder-led companies operate differently on purpose, which can make the signals of a toxic culture difficult to diagnose.

I coached a COO who never expected to work 40-hour weeks. She wanted something closer to 60. Her founder worked 80 to 100, without vacations or days off, and expected the same from his direct reports, because that is what he asked of himself. He expected her to care about the company as much as he did, without the equity that would have made that expectation reasonable.

I helped my client clarify whether this level of effort was due to a temporary build phase or his standard operating model. I also coached her to test whether she could keep up. It turned out that this was his standard operating model, which wasn’t anywhere near sustainable for her, so she ultimately left for a company that was a better match.

If you are trying to work out whether you are in a difficult stretch or part of a true mismatch, the following questions can help:

That last question tends to be the most helpful. If the answer is yes, you’re looking at a structural issue, and trying to adjust on your end won’t change it.

Reporting to a founder often asks more of you than reporting to a typical manager. Test what your founder will actually delegate, map the people they listen to, translate their words before you or your team acts on them and stay honest about whether the mismatch is a stretch or a structure. The executives who do this well build real scope within the space their founder leaves them. You’ve got this!

For more than a decade, founder-led companies have returned more than twice as much to shareholders as companies that are not founder-led, according to Bain. In tech, the multiple is higher still. The executives I speak with take roles at founder-led companies because they’re attracted to high returns. Then they discover the founder will not let go of the work the executive was hired to lead.

I coach C-suite executives who report to founders and co-founders, including COOs, CPOs, CTOs, chiefs of staff and heads of function. I also coach founders themselves, at companies ranging in size from a handful of employees to publicly traded behemoths. Most managing-up advice, my own included, assumes your boss holds a particular role, but this advice doesn’t stick when your founder is running a company they built themselves.

Every founder keeps a short list of tasks they will never hand over, no matter what the organizational chart says, and some of those tasks are likely on your job description.

#5470. Seattle startup OneCourt brings tactile tablets for blind and low-vision fans to NHL games

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 2:01 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 7:00 am

Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.

The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.

The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game.

“Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks, along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.

Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

#5469. I told women to stop chasing balance. Now I’m telling them to ask for help

Alyssa Jaffee is a partner at 7wire Ventures, a venture capital firm investing in digital health companies. She holds board roles at NOCD, MedArrive, Brightline, Zerigo Health, Transcarent, WellTheory and the National Venture Capital Association.

I welcomed my fourth baby on June 29, 2026, six days after writing this. These words capture the week before, when I was 38 weeks pregnant, and the question that kept me awake still feels urgent now.

It was 11 p.m. I was 38 weeks pregnant with my fourth child, and instead of sleeping I was lying in the dark, silently running the list. Camp forms. The pediatrician follow-up. The board deck due to review. Who’s covering carpool the week I deliver? My body was begging me to rest, and my brain wouldn’t let it. By every external measure, I was doing it all. But lately, I could feel myself disappearing.

Four years ago, I wrote an article urging women to stop asking about work-life balance. My advice? You can never be truly balanced. The goal is to live unbalanced, to teeter back and forth, but with conviction about which way you’re leaning. I was pregnant with my third child then, a hustling venture capitalist. Today, I am a mother of four, a growing portfolio behind me, and over three-quarters of a billion dollars raised to deploy into healthcare companies. Now I find myself reflecting on the advice I gave back then. The question I keep asking: did we perfect the art of teetering so well that we forgot to live?

Four kids and a full career later, the list of to-dos is endless. Check one off, move on to the next. Whack-a-mole to the extreme. Focus on optimization. Prioritize. BE EFFICIENT. Get the to-do list done. Don’t worry if I’m the sacrifice.

The mental load has changed from our parents’ generation. Gone are the days when kids ran free until dinner. Unencumbered freedom has been exchanged for meticulous planning. Our kids are overscheduled, and we bear the brunt. And it’s not just the kids. It’s our jobs. The expectation of how much to produce, how high to climb. “How does she do it all?”

And the work never clocks out anymore. Hybrid and remote have blurred the line between the office and the kitchen table until there was no line at all. Now AI promises to make us faster, which somehow just means we’re expected to produce more, around the clock, forever.

But is this having it all? Countless working moms tell me stories of their day, collapsing into bed with just barely enough energy to make it to the following day. We figured out how to live in the unbalance yet it appears we teetered too much, too quickly, and we started losing ourselves in the process.

The trad wife movement has gained steam in part for this reason, a desire for simplicity. It’s not really about sourdough and aprons; it’s a referendum on a deal that stopped working. When “do it all” leaves you this depleted, opting out entirely starts to look like the only way to breathe.

My work as an investor in healthcare companies serving women makes it impossible to ignore: the mental load is exhausting, and it’s measurably hurting women’s health.

Without our health, we have nothing, and women are paying for it.

Mothers carry 71% of the household’s mental load, the invisible work of remembering, planning, anticipating, despite the fact that fathers are more involved than at any point in modern history. They’ve nearly tripled their childcare hours since the 1960s, yet it still isn’t enough.

And that load has a body count. There’s a name for what chronic stress does to a body: allostatic load, the cumulative wear and tear of a stress response that never fully switches off. It’s not a metaphor. It shows up as inflammation, hypertension, and disease, and it’s quietly accruing in women who are praised for how much they can carry.

Women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health than men, roughly nine years each. Nearly half of working women say their job has damaged their mental health in just the past six months. This isn’t fatigue. It’s a deterioration we’ve normalized.

The system that’s supposed to support us isn’t built to. Less than 9% of NIH research dollars over the last decade went to women’s health.

Humans were supposed to be raised in tribes, in community, yet somehow today we are expected to accomplish more than we ever have, in isolation. Please your spouse, take care of your kids, crush it at work, don’t ask for help. In fact, don’t even tell anyone you have help.

A friend of mine was on a panel and was asked how she had four kids. She replied honestly, “I have two nannies and lots of help.” Later she was scolded by the conference organizers, “shhh don’t tell the truth! We don’t want to scare people.”

But isn’t asking for help one of the most important things we can do for ourselves and each other? Somehow, we have lost the ability to be honest and say “I can’t do this alone. I need you.”

I felt that loss too. The optimization of my life was consuming me to the point I lost the greatest gift of all: time. So, I sought out help. First in small, confined ways, and later, more outwardly.

It’s still incredibly difficult. I’m a high-performing woman with local family and resources to pay for help; shouldn’t I be able to do it all?

In the pandemic, I found myself on a text chain with four other women. Half of us had never met in person. Six years later, we’ve texted every single day since, and I consider them some of my closest confidants.

You want to know what we named our chat? The Womb of Silence.

It’s where one of us admits she’s drowning before a board meeting. Where someone asks, with no shame, if anyone has a pediatrician they trust, a therapist taking new patients, a name for the thing they’re feeling or ailment they’re experiencing. Where “I can’t do this alone” is the price of entry, not a confession. Nothing you say there gets you exposed. Nothing gets you judged. You can always ask for help, and someone always answers.

I’ve since replicated this feeling with other groups, my Core of Core and Bad Ass VC Mamas, to name a few.

That chat taught me something the rest of my life kept trying to unteach me: asking isn’t the moment you fail. It’s the moment you actually start living and thriving.

Little by little, I am trying to reframe my brain to believe that doing it all myself doesn’t win me any awards. Deteriorating in plain sight won’t improve my health and happiness. Asking for help will.

The companies I’m drawn to as an investor are the ones giving women back the two things the world keeps taking: their time and their health. Every time I ask for help, I get a little of myself back.

The woman lying awake at 11 p.m., doing it all and quietly disappearing, is starting to reappear. Not because I’m carrying less, but because I’m finally not carrying it alone.

Maybe it’s okay ChatGPT wrote the tooth fairy poem or Instacart auto-ordered my groceries or, gasp, I got a babysitter to take a nap. And as I reflect four years later, with my fourth and final baby now here, I realize that maybe it’s okay to just rest on one side of the see-saw. It’s okay even to climb off of it for a bit to take a break.

Ask for help when you need it. And we all know, we need it.

#5467. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5466. Greenwashing Won’t Save You — How Gen Z Is Rewriting the Rules of Brand Authenticity

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Discover how Gen Z is redefining brand authenticity, challenging greenwashing and demanding transparency, sustainability and real action.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Walk into any corner store or scroll past a sponsored post, and you see it right away. Everything is suddenly “eco-friendly,” “sustainably sourced” or “carbon-neutral.” Companies slap a leaf icon on a plastic wrapper, paint the box olive green and call it a day.

They think this trick still works. It doesn’t.

If your marketing plan leans on empty claims to win over younger buyers, you’re playing a risky game. Greenwashing won’t save your startup. It might actually sink it faster than bad cash flow. Gen Z is rewriting the rules of brand honesty, and they have zero patience for corporate spin.

For two decades, big brands got away with soft marketing. Slap a vague promise about 2050 goals on a billboard, hire a PR agency to write a press release about planting trees and watch sales climb.

Gen Z grew up with a phone in their hand and a search bar at their fingertips. They don’t read your ad copy and take it at face value. They check your supply chain. They search your brand name on TikTok to see if employees are calling out bad workplace habits. They can even look up your parent company’s tax filings.

When a brand gets caught lying about its footprint, the backlash is fast, loud and it doesn’t go away. A fake green label doesn’t make you look responsible. It makes you look dishonest.

Young shoppers don’t expect your startup to be perfect. They know running a business takes resources and that shipping physical goods creates carbon output. What actually bothers them is the theater.

Take a small digital-first startup that sells modular workspace gear. Instead of hiding behind vague terms like “100% Earth-Friendly,” they list the exact components: 80% recycled aluminum, 20% new ABS plastic because of structural limits, made in a factory that runs on a grid with a high coal mix.

That kind of honesty instantly sets them apart from competitors shouting about saving the planet.

Gen Z wants hard facts over soft poetry. They’d rather buy from a business that admits where it falls short than one that pretends to have no flaws at all.

To win customer trust today, startups need to rethink how they talk to people. Here’s how honest brands are changing the story:

Show the receipts: Don’t just say your sourcing is ethical. Prove it. If you run a fast-casual food stall, put the actual invoices from local farm suppliers near your register or post them online every week.

Name the trade-offs: If recycled paper packaging doubles your unit cost and pushes up your retail price, just say so. Customers respect the honesty.

Stop waiting to be perfect: You don’t need a flawless environmental record to speak up. Share your current numbers today, set short-term goals for next month and report back when you fall short.

Modern shoppers know every purchase involves some kind of trade-off. When you pretend your product has zero impact, you insult their intelligence.

Take a modern specialty tea brand as an example. Instead of claiming their tea bags are fully biodegradable, when most actually need industrial composting facilities that regular city systems don’t have, they put a warning label right on the front of the pouch:

“These tea bags need commercial high-heat composting. If you toss them in your garden, they’ll take years to break down. Here’s how to dispose of them the right way.”

That one blunt line builds more brand trust than a million-dollar ad campaign built on fluffy green claims. It shows respect for the buyer’s intelligence.

If you want your business to survive this shift, you need to drop the corporate buzzwords and rebuild how you talk to people, starting now.

Cut words like “green,” “pure,” “natural” and “conscious” from your site unless you back them up with a specific third-party certification or a real number. If a claim can’t be checked, delete it.

Use your social channels to show operational hiccups. If a supplier fails to meet your material standards, post about the delay. Explain why you turned down the shipment. Turn your operational struggles into proof of your standards.

Big-budget, super-polished video ads read as dishonest to an audience raised on user-generated content. A quick, unedited founder video shot on a phone explaining a packaging decision lands far deeper than a slick commercial.

Gen Z isn’t asking every business to solve global problems on its own. They’re asking businesses to stop using those problems as a sales tactic.

If your product is good, let it stand on its own. If your operations are still a work in progress, show the process. Drop the green paint, publish your real numbers and talk to your customers like actual people.

Trust is not something you buy with a clever campaign anymore. It’s something you earn by showing up, dropping the spin and telling the whole truth every single time.

Walk into any corner store or scroll past a sponsored post, and you see it right away. Everything is suddenly “eco-friendly,” “sustainably sourced” or “carbon-neutral.” Companies slap a leaf icon on a plastic wrapper, paint the box olive green and call it a day.

They think this trick still works. It doesn’t.

If your marketing plan leans on empty claims to win over younger buyers, you’re playing a risky game. Greenwashing won’t save your startup. It might actually sink it faster than bad cash flow. Gen Z is rewriting the rules of brand honesty, and they have zero patience for corporate spin.

#5465. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

#5464. Paraguay Bank Collapse Shows Why Bitcoin Was Created as USDT Hits Premium

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Paraguay bank crisis is showing why Bitcoin was created in the first place. USDT sellers reportedly demanded premiums of up to 13% after authorities placed major digital lender Ueno Bank into resolution.

MILLIONS of people LOCKED OUT of their own money as Ueno bank COLLAPSES IN Paraguay President Pena faces IMPEACHMENT — reports pic.twitter.com/3vb8z7MIQm

The crisis left 3 million customers temporarily unable to access their accounts. Some peer-to-peer (P2P) listings showed Tether’s USDT trading around 6,942 Paraguayan guaraníes. That compared with the central bank’s November 4 dollar reference of 6,144.02 guaraníes.

The USDT premium shows growing demand for dollar-denominated assets outside conventional banking. It also revives a question that shaped Bitcoin’s creation: what happens when people cannot freely access money held inside financial institutions?

The Central Bank of Paraguay initiated Ueno Bank’s resolution process on November 3. Regulators found its solvency ratio had fallen below half the legally required minimum following adjustments to its financial statements. Ueno itself had grown rapidly since launching in 2021, becoming one of Paraguay’s most prominent digital lenders.

The bank claimed 3 million customers and managed around $850 million in public funds. Following the intervention, the bank temporarily restricted customer access to accounts and disrupted financial services. Authorities began arranging account transfers and deposit protection while investigators examined the bank’s operations.

The crisis also triggered political fallout. President Santiago Peña announced his resignation on November 5 following mounting pressure over Ueno’s collapse. Reuters reported that prosecutors were investigating him, while authorities issued arrest warrants for eight bank executives.

Meanwhile, the USDT premium attracted attention across cryptocurrency markets. A November 5 review by Criptoinforme examined 80 Binance P2P advertisements. It found that the median price across the 10 best offers for buying USDT stood near 6,399 guaraníes. This represented a 3.4% premium over exchange-house dollar prices.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Paraguay’s banking problems carry an interesting historical connection to Bitcoin’s creation. Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin whitepaper on October 31, 2008, during the global financial crisis. It proposed a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that could transfer value without relying on financial institutions.

The message became even clearer when Nakamoto mined Bitcoin’s genesis block on January 3, 2009. Its embedded newspaper headline read: “Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.”

Bitcoin was designed to address the limitations of a financial system built around trusted intermediaries. Its decentralized network allows users to hold and transfer BTC without requiring permission from a conventional bank.

Paraguay’s situation demonstrates why that proposition still matters. If a bank restricts access to customer accounts, financial independence becomes more than an abstract crypto talking point.

Bitcoin takes another approach through decentralized ownership and self-custody. Users who control their private keys can access their BTC without depending on a bank to authorize withdrawals.

Bitcoin’s original promise was never simply about making investors wealthier. It was about giving people another way to hold and transfer value without depending entirely on the banking system. Paraguay has provided a timely reminder of why that idea emerged in the first place.

#5463. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

#5462. Tech Moves: Fred Hutch leader goes to AWS; Temporal, Augmodo and Neuralwatt name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 6, 2026 at 10:06 amNovember 6, 2026 at 10:45 am

— Amitabha “Guppy” Gupta, a Fred Hutch Cancer Center associate director who helps researchers translate their work to broader audiences, is leaving after 14 years to join Amazon. Starting Nov. 16, he will be a strategic advisor for nonprofit research and advanced AI with AWS’ Global Nonprofit Business.

Gupta said technology was often an obstacle to scientific breakthroughs at Fred Hutch.

“It’s the infrastructure, data, and tools standing between a scientist and an answer,” he wrote on LinkedIn. In his new role, “I’ll work with researchers and research institutions on using cloud, high-performance computing, and AI to remove those barriers.”

— Microsoft board member ‌Emma Walmsley has been appointed CEO of HP, effective Jan. 4. Walmsley, who led the pharmaceutical giant GSK until December 2025, succeeds Bruce Broussard. Reuters notes that her seven years serving on the Microsoft board “are her closest brush with the tech sector” prior to taking the top job at the PC maker.

— Bas Nijholt, senior staff engineer at IonQ‘s Seattle-area facility, has resigned after three years to join an AI startup that’s still in stealth mode. At IonQ, the theoretical quantum mechanics expert built MindRoom, an open-source collaboration and knowledge-sharing platform that he calls “a company brain.”

“With this new opportunity, I get to keep building and turbocharging MindRoom with a team of people who are just as excited about AI as I am,” Nijholt said, adding that the tool will remain freely available.

Before IonQ, Nijholt spent nearly four years at Microsoft.

— Bellevue, Wash., startup Temporal, whose software keeps AI agents running reliably, has named Sean Heneghan as vice president of sales for the Americas. The company ranks No. 1 on the GeekWire 200, a list of the top Pacific Northwest startups. In September it raised $550 million, putting its valuation at $12.55 billion.

Temporal is fully remote, and Heneghan is based in the Chicago area. He joins the company from MongoDB.

— Doug Heimburger, a 26-year Amazon veteran, has changed roles, shifting from chief financial officer and vice president of Worldwide Operations to CFO/VP of Worldwide Stores. In the new position, Heimburger said he’ll help oversee efforts to improve delivery speed, reduce costs and increase growth of the Stores business. His first role at the company was data mining analyst.

— Seattle startup Augmodo has named Capri Brixey as head of retail sales. The company, which sells AI-powered wearable devices with cameras, raised $21 million in July to expand from in-store applications that let workers passively track inventory into automotive, warehouse and hospital settings. Augmodo ranks No. 122 on the GeekWire 200.

Ross Finman, founder and CEO of Augmodo, called Brixey “the right leader to accelerate our expansion” given her experience selling to both retail and warehouse operations. Her past roles include leadership positions at Coca-Cola and Kroger.

— Meaghan Davison Praznik was named vice president of marketing for Neuralwatt, a Seattle-based startup that built a tool for calculating, in real time, the carbon emissions of individual AI requests. Her former employers include Clif Bar, AllTrails and Merino Energy.

Because the carbon intensity of grid power varies throughout the day and across regions, Neuralwatt’s technology can help customers run compute-intensive operations when clean energy is more abundant.

— BuyWander, an auction-based online marketplace for returned and overstocked retail items, has named Chris Holm as senior director of product. Holm spent nine years at Amazon, leaving in 2024 after managing last-mile and same-day delivery technology and working on Amazon Fresh delivery. He has since served as a consultant for carbon removal startup Lithos Carbon and as a founder-in-residence at the startup studio Foundations.

In August, BuyWander moved its headquarters across Washington from Spokane to Kent. The company announced $21 million in new funding in September.

— T-Mobile’s Kevin Lau has joined the advisory board at the University of Washington’s College of Engineering. Lau has been with the telecom giant for 22 years over two stints and serves as VP of digital experience engineering. He holds bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the UW.

— Christian Smith, an Issaquah, Wash.-based tech leader, has been named president of revenue for Cloudflare, which provides security and speed services for websites and online applications. He will oversee worldwide go-to-market operations. Smith previously served as chief revenue officer for Splunk and Nintex.

#5461. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

Hope you have a stellar weekend! If you haven’t signed up for our upcoming event on November 13th, don’t wait too long.
